#6744. This Olympic Volleyball Player’s Kona Village Wedding Was a Heartfelt Tribute to His Hawaiian Roots

As two UCLA volleyball players, Susannah Muno and Micah Ma’a often crossed paths. “The athlete community at UCLA was pretty tight-knit, so we ran into each other here and there. But we were never really in the same circles,” says Susannah, who goes by Zana. It wasn’t until a dare during their senior year that they truly connected. “I remember so vividly being on the bus with my team during a road trip when I got an Instagram DM from Micah. I screamed,” she says. “Naturally, I passed my phone around to the entire team, and then we all screamed.” It turns out that Micah and two teammates each chose someone for the others to DM. “Very college,” laughs Zana. “Three girls on our team got DMs from three guys on the men’s team that day. Two of those three couples are still together.”

Micah’s friends clearly put fate into motion. Zana and Micah made plans to see each other and that first night, they talked, laughed, and even cried until morning. “Somewhere in the middle of that night, I realized that how hot he was was actually the least interesting thing about him,” says Zana. “I won’t go so far as to say it was love at first sight. But I do think that from that first day together, we both knew there wasn’t really a version of our lives where we didn’t want the other person in it.”

Over the next six years, the two navigated a long-distance relationship as they competed professionally around the world. Micah even represented the United States at the 2024 Paris Olympics and helped the Indoor Volleyball team win a bronze medal. Two weeks later, on August 19th, 2024, Micah proposed. “We drove our little golf cart to dinner at a restaurant in our beach town that I had been wanting to try all summer,” recalls Zana. “After dinner, we went for a walk along the beach, as we often do, and that’s when it happened!” The couple celebrated at home together in their “own little bubble of happiness.” Family and friends helped them pull together an engagement party in just a few days to celebrate. “The very next day, Micah and I packed our bags and left for his next season abroad—a pretty fitting start to the next chapter of our lives,” she says.

The couple decided to tie the knot on May 24, 2026, in Kona Village on the Big Island of Hawai’i. “Micah is Native Hawaiian, and his Hawaiian culture is something deeply rooted within him and his family,” explains Zana. “Having the privilege of getting married on the island of Hawaiʻi, on land that feels so raw, untouched, and sacred, was something we didn’t take lightly. Throughout the entire planning process, we wanted to honor and respect the culture of this land and its people. We kept coming back to one simple vision for the wedding: a sense of place.”

Curating a thoughtful group of vendors made this dream come to life. Alison Rose Events managed planning, while the bride and her future sister-in-law helped lead the design process. “I spent so much time finding the right people—people who felt like family and, in many cases, actually were,” says Zana. “Each of our musicians was a friend of the family, which made every space feel that much more intimate. It wasn’t a stranger playing a violin; it was a friend sharing his gift with us on one of the most meaningful days of our lives.”

Florals, in particular, were a key part of their wedding weekend’s vision. Ren MacDonald-Balasia of Renko Floral foraged greenery and blooms from all over the island—including some family members’ backyards—to create organic arrangements that felt true to the environment. Lei worn throughout the weekend were also hand-made by Micah’s family. “None of these details were about creating something simply for the sake of beauty,” says Zana. “They were about making the weekend feel like us and, just as importantly, making it feel like Hawaiʻi.”

With a full weekend of celebration planned throughout Kona Village, the couple needed to fill their wardrobes with the perfect pieces for each event. Zana looked back in her closet for her first bridal look. “Micah and I actually got legally married the year before at Kona Village with just the two of us and our officiant,” says the bride. “I wore a Hanne Bloch two-piece silk tulle set, and we stood barefoot on the lanai of our hale as we said our vows. When it came time to choose what I would wear to our welcome party exactly one year later, it felt only right to wear that same outfit again.” The groom also donned a piece from the past for the party, choosing to wear his Tūtū’s (grandfather’s) aloha shirt as a nostalgic touch.

The next day was full of activities, starting with a pickleball tournament with a Wimbledon white dress code. The bride wore a matching Alo set and popped on a custom hat the couple had made for all their guests. “Of course, Micah won,” says Zana. “I’m still not sure his partner touched a single ball, but that’s beside the point.” The couple then spent the afternoon poolside with all their guests. Zana kept it carefree in a Monday Swimwear bikini with a Solaqua cover-up. “We had fresh coconuts filled with a little rum float, lounged around the pool, and eventually ended up taking one huge group swim out to the lily pad in the ocean,” she says.

The bride’s next ensemble made a bigger statement. “For our rehearsal dinner, I wore a shell-and-fringe dress by British designer Kilentar that weighed 22 pounds,” Zana says. “The dress was everything that night was: fun, organic, flirty, and a little unexpected. It floated and moved so beautifully, and with literally every step I took, the shells made the most incredible sound.” Micah complemented her natural-toned look in a custom linen button-down and trousers.

Zana at first struggled to find a dress for the wedding day until Danielle Frankel opened her bridal boutique in Los Angeles. “I tried on my dress just days after it had come down the runway, and immediately, my mind was made up,” she says of her strapless gown. “The organic, lightweight linen fabric mirrored the textures of the landscape around us, while the bubble hem gave the dress this beautiful shape and movement that reminded me of the ocean and the lava rock.” Micah had one request for Zana’s bridal ensemble: he asked her to wear a veil. A style from Danielle Frankel was the perfect fit. “I loved it so much that I vowed to myself she will be worn again,” she says.

For Micah’s walk down the aisle, he had a bespoke suit made at The Imperial Tailoring Company in Moscow. “He had been away for the eight months leading up to the wedding, so having a suit made together in the U.S. simply wasn’t possible,” explains Zana. “Instead, we set out to find the best tailor we could in Russia and ended up creating the most incredible custom suit for him.” She adds, “In a funny way, even his wedding look became a reflection of the life we were living at the time.”

During the reception, Zana had two outfit changes. First, she wore a mini dress that was crafted from the skirt of her mother’s wedding dress. “Wearing a piece of my mother’s dress was so much more emotional than I anticipated,” she reflects. Her final look was an Elce linen two-piece set with a backless halter top and pants. “It was very me—comfortable, freeing, and effortless,” Zana says.

Zana’s jewelry throughout the weekend was actually all pieces borrowed from her mother’s best friend, Lisa Wehrly, whom the bride sees as a mentor and role model. “I was able to wear pieces from her collection throughout the celebrations, each one carrying its own stories and history,” she says.

The celebrations kicked off on Friday night with a casual welcome event overlooking the ocean. Cocktails, bites, and conversation led to an unexpected turn. “In classic Hawaiian get-together fashion, it wasn’t long before someone picked up a microphone,” says Zana. “Micah’s sister, Mehana Maʻa, took the mic for a few songs, followed by Micah himself, who sang ‘I’m Yours’ by Jason Mraz. He then somehow transitioned into a hilarious, completely off-the-cuff freestyle, welcoming everyone to this beautiful place and telling them to get ready for the best weekend. Everyone absolutely erupted. It was spontaneous and so perfectly Micah, and it immediately set the tone for the weekend.”

The next day was filled with pickleball, poolside drinks, and connection under the Hawaiian sun. Then, the night turned more intimate with a rehearsal dinner in a Kiawe grove with an open-air barbecue. The couple, who love to host, wanted the evening to feel like a night at their home with speeches added in. “Of course, Micah and I decided it was necessary to make our way around dinner, taking a shot with every single table,” says Zana. “Needless to say, the energy escalated pretty quickly. Everyone loosened up, we ate incredible food, laughed all night, and had the absolute best time.”

However, the night didn’t end just yet. The couple and friends piled into golf carts back to their villa. “The second I walked through the door, my 22-pound dress hit the floor, and everyone jumped straight into the pool in their clothes. I opted for slightly less clothing and did a little skinny-dipping,” says Zana. “My mom and dad came out of bed and jumped in wearing their pajamas, while my brother and the rest of our family were mildly appalled that I was completely naked. It was chaotic and ridiculous and absolutely perfect.” She adds, “It will forever be one of my favorite memories from the weekend.”

The ceremony took place the next day on the black sand beach surrounded by lava rock and cliffs overlooking the ocean. “It was dramatic. It was raw. It was perfect,” describes Zana. The bride walked down the aisle with her father to “Somewhere Over the Rainbow,” and Micah’s best friend Evan Enriques officiated the proceedings. “The vows were, without question, the heart of it all,” remembers the bride. “There was nothing gentle or lighthearted about them. They were genuine and from the heart—raw and unfiltered, just like the place where we stood. From what we’ve heard since the wedding, there wasn’t a dry eye in sight.” The couple both felt as if everything else fell away and they were speaking to each other from the heart. “It was one of the best moments of my life,” says the bride.

The reception kicked off with cocktail hour, followed by dinner and dancing. “Micah’s seven-year-old niece opened dinner with a prayer in ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi, which was such a special way to begin the evening,” says Zana. Speeches were followed by a hula performance by Micah’s three sisters and niece, then a fire knife dance from the groom’s best friend, Larry “Tui” Tuileta. “Before long, Micah and Evan had joined him,” says Zana. Watching the three of them together was so special because this wasn’t something created for the wedding—they have been doing versions of this at family parties since they were little.”

“The rest of the night is honestly a blur in the best possible way,” says the bride. Dancing was followed by another late-night jump into the pool at the villa after-party. “Eventually, it was just Micah and me and a handful of our closest friends sitting around the dinner table, talking until four in the morning. A couple of them stayed so late that they left the table and headed almost directly to the airport for their flights home.”

“It felt like the perfect way to end the weekend,” adds the bride. “We’re just heartbroken that we can’t do it all over again!”

Exactly one year before our welcome party, Micah and I were legally married at Kona Village, just the two of us. It felt only right to rewear the stunning Hanne Bloch silk tulle two-piece set I wore that day. I’m so glad I did. It was such a special way to bring a piece of that intimate day into our wedding weekend. —Zana

It’s happening! I remember walking up to the Moana Lawn and thinking, “Oh my gosh, it’s really here.” Seeing everything I had envisioned come to life brought this incredible combination of relief and excitement. Suddenly, it was all real. —Zana

I wanted our welcome flowers to be inspired by the plumeria flower lei so often given upon arriving in Hawaiʻi. To make this vision come to life, our florist, Ren MacDonald-Balasia, went down to Kealakekua and met with a very special retired gardener who let her cut and purchase blooms directly from her yard. She had the longest oncidium orchids growing out of the lava rock wall that were about 36 inches a stem. She used them like vines and wove them through the butter yellow shower-tree blooms to create an unexpected arrangement of yellow en masse—intentionally combined together to invoke curiosity, like it could be one flower, not two. —Zana

My grandma and one of my best friends, hand-in-hand and cocktail in hand. Exactly the spirit we were hoping for all weekend! —Zana

This photo captures the pure joy I felt watching all of my favorite people arrive for our wedding weekend. Savannah is my childhood best friend, and I had the privilege of standing beside her during her own magical wedding celebrations. Now it was my turn. There is something so special about moving through life’s biggest chapters alongside the people who have known you the longest. —Zana

In nearly every childhood photo I have with my mom, I’m holding on tight. She’s always meant the world to me. Living overseas means I don’t get to hug her nearly as often as I’d like, so when I do, I never take it for granted. —Micah

Are you kidding?! The sunset, the people, the weather, the place, and THAT MAN! No words will ever do it justice. —Zana

In this moment, I remember feeling exactly the way I used to in college while watching Micah play volleyball at UCLA. His charisma and energy are unlike anything I’ve ever experienced, and I think everyone there was completely charmed by him in that moment. It was just so perfectly Micah. —Zana

This photo captures my wife perfectly. Her joy, her spirit, and her enthusiasm for life. —Micah

My niece has been asking her mom nonstop if she can please go back to Uncle Micah and Aunty Zana’s wedding. I’m not sure anyone had a better time than she did. —Micah

Everyone hard at work putting together their scouting reports.

Obviously, Micah won pickleball. And no, nobody took it easy on him. —Zana

For our save-the-dates, I embroidered our wedding details onto the same linen my dress was made from. They simply read, “Micah and Susannah – Kona Village, HI – May 24, 2026.” My Grandma Sue, never one to miss an opportunity, used hers to customize her hat for the pickleball tournament. —Zana

I’m pretty sure I didn’t stop smiling the entire weekend! —Zana

We’re a competitive bunch, so naturally, we had to hire legitimate referees for our pickleball tournament. —Micah

The long farm tables, the warmth of the fire, and the soft lighting made the evening feel less like a formal rehearsal dinner and more like a family dinner in our own home.

We wanted the florals to feel like a celebration of Hawaiʻi. Our florist Ren sourced rare bromeliad blooms that were punctuated by ripe and shiny mountain apples that were sourced from the Hilo farmer’s market. She wanted the arrangements to invoke a sense of lava flowing through the rocks, so in addition to the fiery color palette, she used hala lei made from the pandanus fruit to slope down the actual lava rocks at the base of the piece.

Hand in hand, on our way to the rehearsal dinner. —Micah

My beautiful mother made a special lei from naupaka, the flower we had chosen as the symbol of our wedding. —Micah

My two younger sisters gave such an amazing speech, starting the night off in a way that made it feel like one big family dinner. People reminisced about old times and our stories became even grander than the last time we had told them. —Micah

My relationship with my sisters has never been a rollercoaster full of highs and lows. Instead, for as long as I can remember, it has been a steady source of the most loyal and loving support that I have experienced. —Micah

I feel like one of the luckiest people in the world to have parents who have supported every dream I’ve ever had. My wedding was no exception. Watching my dad beam as he saw me living out my fairy-tale wedding meant everything to me. —Zana

I might be biased, but this was one of the best meals of my life! The warmth of the fire, the local vegetables, and a family-style dinner beneath the lights and trees. I’ll never get over it. —Zana

Our niece and goddaughter loved my Kilentar shell-and-fringe dress just as much as I did! I remember seeing it for the first time and thinking, “This isn’t a want. It’s a need!” —Zana

A wedding-morning canoe ride—just the two of us!

The ocean has always been such an important place for us. It’s a place of healing and a place of cleansing. Before we make a big move across the world or a big decision in life, we have always made sure to jump in the water. —Micah

She sells seashells by the seashore. And he buys them just to spend a little more time with her. —Micah

Growing up, The Parent Trap was my all-time favorite movie. There’s a scene at camp where they’re raising and lowering the flag that has always stuck with me. When we started dreaming up our wedding weekend, I wanted it to have that same nostalgic feeling of summer camp. And, of course, no summer camp would be complete without a flag. —Zana

Seeing my wedding dress hanging beside the mini dress made from my mother’s wedding gown was incredibly meaningful. My parents’ marriage is something I’ve always admired and aspired to, and having such a special piece of their wedding day woven into my own felt like a beautiful full-circle moment. —Zana

The most incredible human I’ve ever known. My mom. —Zana

From the moment Micah and I met, we shared the same greatest priority in life: our families. So when it came time to decide who I wanted around me while getting ready, the answer felt obvious. I wanted to be surrounded by the women who have shaped my life. They wore the most beautiful House of Pacific dresses, while I got ready in a Danielle Frankel robe. —Zana

The dramatic contrast of my billowing white Danielle Frankel gown against the jagged black lava still takes my breath away. —Zana

The two men who have lifted me up and carried me through every chapter of my life. —Zana

Moments before walking down the aisle. I was more nervous than I’d expected. I think the magnitude of what was about to happen finally caught up with me. —Zana

One of the greatest gifts God has ever given me is this man. My father. —Micah

I found this suit in an underground shop near Red Square in Moscow. The story is far too long to tell, as so many of our stories from living overseas tend to be. But getting married in Hawaiʻi wearing a suit I found in Russia just about sums up our lives. —Micah

Micah and I had originally chosen another ceremony location on the property, but the moment we saw this spot, we knew our plans had to change. The drama of the black lava against the crashing blue waves felt like the perfect setting for this chapter of our story. —Zana

We wanted the ceremony florals to feel as though they were growing naturally from the landscape, complementing the beauty of the island rather than competing with it. Our florist so beautifully juxtaposed the sharpness of local foraged Kona grasses with the softness of cream colored oncidium orchids. The grasses created waves while the orchids created fluttering foamy moments, indicative of the ocean behind the ceremony.

Our guests making their way to the ceremony.

I have dreamt of this moment hundreds of times since I was a little girl. I always imagined my dad would cry because, if you know him, you know he’s a big softie. But somehow, neither of us did. Instead, we laughed and smiled in complete disbelief at just how perfect everything felt. —Zana

I’ve never experienced a moment where I was so completely unaware of everything else happening in the world. Watching your future wife walk down the aisle is a feeling that can’t really be explained. It’s something you can only understand once you’ve experienced it. —Micah

Whenever someone asks me about my favorite moment of the weekend, I don’t have to think twice. It was sharing our vows. —Zana

There is no better feeling than knowing the people you love most absolutely adore the man you’re about to marry. —Zana

Smiles, tears, laughter, and so much love. This ceremony had it all.

In true Parent Trap fashion, we recessed down the aisle to Natalie Cole’s “This Will Be.”

Just two kids who fell in love and never looked back.

I asked Ren, our florist, for a cascading bouquet with just a hint of color and left everything else in her hands. As she did so many times throughout the weekend, she absolutely blew me away with what she created.

Micah’s hands have always been one of my favorite things about him. Seeing a wedding ring on his finger felt completely surreal. —Zana

A poolside cocktail hour overlooking the black lava and deep blue sea.

The brother of the bride clearly had no fun at all! —Zana

Round tables beneath the palms, soft white linens, and the ocean in the distance made for the most beautiful setting for dinner.

For the reception, Ren carried the natural beauty of the island through to our dinner tables. The tables were full of symbolism and native material. One of the most special symbols were the Naupaka branches and flowers, an ode to the Hawaiian legend of Naupaka and the symbol we chose to represent their wedding. There was also local gardenia from Oahu on every table, a very special flower to Micah’s family. The gardenia were hand carried on the plane, and the extra effort to bring them over was worth it as their fragrance wafted through the reception tables with each passing Kona breeze. —Zana

I’ve always loved making things—particularly embroidery and sewing—so I created these hardcover menus myself, embroidering each guest’s name onto the linen cover. —Zana

A bare statement piece that blends so seamlessly into the surrounding environment while still making a statement.

Quite possibly my favorite photo of Micah ever. —Zana

We both come from long lines of storytellers, so when someone in the family gets hold of a microphone, you know it’s showtime.

Aside from marrying the love of my life, this was the most emotional moment of the entire weekend for me. My sisters mean everything to me. It’s always been the four of us. They’ve danced hula since we were kids, and having them dance for us and—in their own way—bless our marriage was incredibly moving. It was the second time that day I cried. —Micah

My lifelong best friend has been fire-knife dancing at our family parties since we were eight years old. There was no way we could end our wedding night without him performing, just as he always has for us. He’s one of the most talented people I know, and man, can he spin those sticks! —Micah

Ending the night the only way we saw fit.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday offer equally good clothing deals. Plan for large retailers and more-established brands to offer deals on Black Friday, and smaller menswear boutiques to hold out for Cyber Monday. As a baseline, expect the better Black Friday sales to start at 20% off and go upwards from there. In the lead up to Black Friday, also be on the lookout for the coveted sale on sale, which has become the norm in recent years.

#6740. Understated, Earthy, and Endlessly Wearable: The Best Olive Green Polishes

The earthy shade adds an edge to fall manicures while still wearing like a neutral.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Like all nail polish colors, green has a vast spectrum, one that runs from electric neon to bold kelly to soft sage and all the way down to deep, moody olive. Of all the greens out there, olive sits in a quieter place. The hue is earthy and a little mysterious, somewhere between a vintage army jacket and an actual juicy olive. It’s a shade we love for fall, since it pairs so seamlessly with black, rich browns, burgundy, red, and, of course, cream.

Once reserved for the brave few, olive has now gone mainstream. Part of the appeal is how wearable it is, offering an unexpected twist without ever feeling too loud. It’s also soft and soothing to the eye, making it an easy shade to wear day after day.

If you’re new to the shade, the easiest way in is to treat it like a neutral. Try it with a camel coat and chunky knits when the weather turns, or a crisp white shirt for something fresh and unexpected. A creamy, opaque finish feels polished and modern, while a glossy jelly or a hint of shimmer adds depth in low light. However you wear it, olive looks effortlessly considered and adds an edge to your style.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best olive green nail polishes to shop now.

A personal favorite, Elia is a muted olive green that looks rich from the very first stroke. The opaque formula glides on evenly in a single swipe and dries to a soft gloss that lasts through daily wear.

Manucurist’s take on olive green feels a touch brighter. It sits beautifully on light and dark skin tones alike and delivers an opaque wash of color. Part of the “Green Flash” collection, it cures under an LED gel lamp and lasts for nearly 21 days.

Essie’s Totally Plaid is an olive green polish with a cream finish that delivers a gel-like shine and depth while still removing as easily as a regular polish. The formula applies smoothly in two coats, giving you rich, opaque color without the need for a UV lamp.

This deep and moody olive green shade is the epitome of effortless chic, pairing easily with everything from neutral knits to bold jewel tones.

Inspired by the lush landscapes of the Mediterranean, this olive green evokes a lighter take on the olive color spectrum. It’s a tad brighter and slightly more yellow-toned, making it a great pick if you want a fresh, sunlit green this fall.

O.P.I’s Suzi is the chic olive green and wardrobe staple of the olive family. It’s a bit darker-toned, radiating earthy warmth and understated elegance. Plus, it’s fast-drying and offers up to seven days of wear.

For those seeking a little more sparkle, this olive green jelly is packed with large green holographic glitters that create a textured finish and catch the light with every movement, adding a spark of joy to your manicure.

Calming and serene, this moss green shade is part of the “Campground Collection”, a four-shade assortment of earthy, comforting colors. Its buttery-smooth application matches the shade’s peaceful look.

This may not look like your average olive green at first glance, but that’s because it has taupe undertones. Once it’s on your nails, you’ll notice the hint of green was there all along. The result is a soft, grounded neutral that pairs effortlessly with cozy fall knits and earthy accessories.

This nail color may be named Pickle, but we see the olive in there. This tangy green with muted yellow undertones feels lively while remaining neutral enough to pair with everything in your wardrobe.

A true olive green, Extra Dirty brings rich, earthy depth to your nails. All you need is one to two coats for a creamy manicure worthy of a fall-season spotlight.

#6737. JFK Jr.’s ’94 Saab Is Up for Auction. You Should Buy It

The late John F. Kennedy Jr., in addition to being the subject of countless menswear moodboards, a hit Ryan Murphy series, and, hey, a new coffee table book written by yours truly, was one of the most stylish guys in 1990s New York. Between his American-dynasty pedigree, chiseled good looks, and impossibly thick head of hair, not to mention his eclectic wardrobe of preppy classics, funky gorpcore, and Armani suits, it’s not hard to see why. It should come as no surprise, then, that he also had excellent taste in cars. Throughout the ’90s, JFK Jr.’s whip of choice was a 1994 Saab 900 SE Coupe, a quirky Swedish sports car that embodied everything that was great about ’90s style, down to its hunter green paint. Fortunately, for fans of oddball vintage autos and JFK Jr. alike, it’s currently up for sale via RR Auction, and the bids are rolling in.

Sporty, sophisticated, and eccentric, the Saab 900 was to JFK Jr. what the pink Cadillac Fleetwood was to Elvis, or the Porsche 935 was to Paul Newman. An consummate outlier in the American car market since the ’50s, Saab’s popularity peaked in the mid-1980s when its weird, angular designs and quirks(e.g., the ignition was next to the handbrake) found a following among design-obsessed American yuppies. Combining the Scandinavian sobriety of a Volvo with the postmodern flair of a Memphis sofa, Saab loomed large in ’90s culture: Jerry Seinfeld’s TV alter-ego drove one, as did Niles Crane, Dana Scully, and Clark Griswald’s humorless neighbors in National Lampoon’s Christmas Vacation.

During the tail end of the decade, when JFK Jr. and his late wife, publicist Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, were fixtures of Lower Manhattan life, the couple was frequently photographed driving in the Saab near their Tribeca loft. With its sporty-yet-economical turbocharged four-cylinder engine, a sleek leather interior, and a custom set of aftermarket aqua-blue padded ski racks mounted to the roof, it embodied JFK Jr.’s characteristic blend of aristocratic, athletic, and bohemian to a tee.

JFK Jr.'s green 1994 Saab 900 SE, with a current bid of nearly $30,000 and rising.

According to Bobby Livingston, executive vice president at RR Auction, “what makes this lot so special is it's not some Maserati or something flashy like that—it's a practical car that was a part of his everyday life. For Kennedy, “the choice of this car, as opposed to a Mercedes or something, speaks a lot to his style.” This particular Saab—which JFK Jr. purchased new from Zumbach Sports Cars in Manhattan for $29,841.21 in the summer of 1994, and owned until his death in 1999—comes to auction via Kevin J. Hynes, a screenwriter and longtime friend of Kennedy’s who worked with him at the New York DA’s office in the early ’90s. According to the auction listing, the car had been left at Hynes’s Westchester home in the days following Kennedy’s fatal plane crash. In 2000, Hynes then bought the car from the Kennedy estate in 2000 for $6,000, and sold it for $12,000 two years later. Its third owner is said to have started up the car regularly, but judging by its overall condition and the looks of its odometer, which shows just 30,650 miles, it seems it hasn’t hit the road in a long time.

The Saab, which was listed with a minimum sale price of $15,000, is part of a RR’s Fine Autographs and Artifacts auction that also includes a tweed hat worn by the elder JFK and Lee Harvey Oswald’s overcoat. As of Wednesday afternoon, more than 20 bids have driven the price close to $30,000. “We’ve sold a Hummer that belonged to Tupac, and a Cadillac Escalade that was used by Tony Soprano in The Sopranos, but I didn't know there would be such an affection for John F. Kennedy Jr.’s Saab,” says Livingston. “It’s already exceeded our estimate, and there’s a lot of interest, so it could go for a lot more than where it is right now.”

The Kennedys, seen here in 1998, were frequently seen driving in the Saab near their Tribeca loft.

Given its provenance and climbing auction price tag, whether JFK Jr.’s Saab ends up with a car collector, a Kennedy buff, or someone with a keen appreciation for peak-1990s style, one hopes that whoever buys it will be well-equipped to give it the treatment it deserves. That is to say, this is a car that deserves to be street-parked in Tribeca, driven to Vermont for ski trips, and otherwise treated like the ’90s style icon it is. A backward Kangol cap and an “I TOLD YA” tee are optional, but highly recommended.

#6736. The Latest Look at Taylor Swift’s Off-Duty Style Comes With a New Detail About Her Wedding

Taylor Swift has flown under the radar for most of the fall, only making public appearances at her husband Travis Kelce’s home games and a few industry events. Yesterday, however, fans got a new look at Swift’s casual, off-duty style in an unexpected place: the Hancock County Humane Foundation’s Instagram. The animal welfare nonprofit shared a photo of Swift and Kelce with Kelce’s longtime agent, Mike Simon, and his wife Lisa Marie, who attended their wedding. The post revealed a new detail about the newlyweds’ request to guests in lieu of giving them gifts.

“Four beautiful people, four generous hearts,” the West Virginia-based organization wrote. “The Hancock County Humane Foundation is honored to acknowledge a very generous donation from Attorney Mike Simon and his wife Lisa in honor of a very special wedding they recently attended. The amazing bride and groom asked for donations to charities in lieu of gifts and Mike and Lisa chose us!!”

Swift appeared to be wearing the red Tommy Hilfiger cable-knit polo she wore during Kelce’s game on Sunday with baggy, light-wash jeans.

The post came hours after The Hollywood Reporter revealed Swift would be receiving the Sherry Lansing Leadership Award at its Women in Entertainment Gala. Greta Gerwig will present the honor to her, which “recognizes trailblazers and philanthropists in entertainment and media and was established in honor of Sherry Lansing, the first woman to head a Hollywood studio,” the outlet wrote.

“Taylor Swift took on an industry that has long underestimated women and won on every front: artistically, commercially, and on the question of who owns her work,” the publication’s editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, said. “She reclaimed her catalog, set new terms for the artists who follow her, and became the most popular musician in the world while doing it—and helping scores of other artists along the way. We’re proud to honor her with the Sherry Lansing Leadership Award.”

#6733. Zimmermann Hosts a Star-Studded Soirée in Downtown New York City

Katie Holmes, Uma Thurman, and Naomi Watts came out to celebrate the brand’s cruise 2027 collection.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Inside Indochine’s red-lit, retro-inspired French-Vietnamese dining room in New York City, Zimmermann gathered friends of the brand to celebrate its cruise 2027 collection. Presented on the sun-drenched Côte d’Azur in June, the label’s latest served as the perfect bit of vacation and occasion-ready dressing for November in New York. Now that the lineup has officially hit stores, fashion insiders and fans of the brand alike (including Uma Thurman, Eve Hewson, Katie Holmes, and Naomi Watts) showed up dripping in ruffled gowns, sailor-inspired stripes, chunky shearlings, and ethereal lace and silks from the collection. Against the dark, 1940s-inspired tropical salon interior of Indochine, it was the ideal mix of downtown energy and New York glamour.

As champagne flowed through the bar area, glasses clinked while miniature crab cakes and spring rolls were passed. Zimmermann’s sister duo Nicky and Simone Zimmermann could be spotted catching up with friends new and old. “We have a very, very close connection with New York,” Nicky told ELLE in between greeting guests. “It was pretty much when I started the business, one of the first places internationally that I went to in the ’90s, and it blew my mind. It’s been inspirational to us 100 percent.” It was a rare occasion for the brand; for years, Zimmermann has shown at Paris Fashion Week (after presenting in New York in the mid-2010s) and the duo oscillates between Sydney and Paris for most of the year.

Zimmermann’s painterly and intrinsically bohemian flourishes could be seen in the many outfits of guests, all highlighting the vivid cruise collection. Think: decadent silky draped drop-waisted gowns and paneled lace maxi dresses, or, for the more demure, sleek all-black looks that captured the New York essence. “For me, there’s a little bit of a sense of humor behind it—without insulting anybody—it was about the story when Australia actually beat America in the America’s Cup, which is a very famous sailing race,” Nicky told ELLE of the collection’s inspiration.

“I think it was in 1983, and America had not lost the America’s Cup in something like 173 years; it was a ridiculous winning streak, and Australia came along. The inspiration is more about a David and Goliath kind of story,” she continued. “We came along as the Aussies, not established in the sailing world. They were very cheeky, rogue, kind of Aussie young guys up against this amazing, sophisticated establishment of the New York Yacht Club. And they never lost—and we beat them. So in Australia, it’s a legendary story.” Nicky combined the sportiness of sailing gear with the sort of elite New York Yacht Club preppiness, resulting in colorful silk scarf embellishment or sweaters decked out in accessorized pins. “They would hold the most incredible parties and the women were so glamorous and sophisticated and beautiful and not anything that Australia could relate to at the time, so I loved the contrast.”

Conversation was flowing and blooming anthuriums covered the tables as guests took their seats. Nicky kicked off the dinner with a speech, musing on her early days in New York on the Lower East Side and the many parties she attended in Tribeca before sharing more inspiration behind the collection: “It’s about establishment, and then it’s about people, you know, working really hard, coming together as a team, defeating the undefeatable,” she said, with a laugh.

Next came an intimate performance by the singer and Bad Monkey actress Charlotte Lawrence, who sang two of her original songs, then led a folksy sing-along to “Dreams” by Fleetwood Mac. Even the most guarded of celebs and fashion’s elite couldn’t help but bob their heads and sing a tune. As guests dined on a family-style mix of kale salad, spicy shrimp, grilled salmon, barbecued chicken, and steak, the champagne glass clinks slowed as candles slowly flickered and the evening closed out with lemon tarts.

A little yacht-club polish, a little Aussie irreverence: Zimmermann celebrated cruise 2027 in high style.

#6731. 26 Best Men's Scarves 2026, According to GQ Editors

Are any accessories as essential, yet mysteriously overlooked, as the best men's scarves? First, they warm your neck (and face, and chest) like nothing else. Second, they put a style-forward, cheery, colorful bow on pretty much any outfit. And yet, these soft little miracles are all too often an afterthought in the menswear world. Even if you’re the type of guy to painstakingly lay your fits out the night before, chances are when it comes to your scarf game, you’re still reaching for one you picked up in a rushed pinch from Nordstrom Rack, or at a frigid college football game.

This is, of course, fine. But it’s also sort of a tragedy. Because when you pick up a truly great scarf, everything changes. Swaddling your neck in cashmere (or cashmere-emulating fabrics) doesn’t just provide a soothing all-day embrace through bracing winds. It also, like a necktie, creates an opportunity for a flash of personal style, right under your handsome face. Even better, because scarves use less fabric than coats and knitwear, they’re also a great way to own some of the best materials in our industry for far less scratch.

To help you pick the one you’ll soon be recognized by, I surveyed hundreds of scarves from across the fashion (and budget) spectrum, journeying from mall chains, to historic British manufacturers, to the buzziest makers today, and everything in-between. Below, the final 26 best men's scarves to knot up this winter—and next winter, and the one after that.

Parisian label Brut puts a Big Apple spin on the classic European football supporter scarf, featuring none other than Lady Liberty herself. A fitting French connection.

The bandana, neckerchief, foulard, whatever you want to call it has become an easy, even trendy winter accessory. Alex Mill’s is made from extra-fine merino wool, comes in 14 colors, and costs less than a hundo.

Another bandana-shaped style from the Banana, this time with a generous helping of cashmere for a little extra softness.

A smart tartan plaid as classic as the linings inside Barbour’s famous wax jackets, in a soft wool-cashmere blend. About as British as a rainy afternoon and a pint at the pub.

We cross the Irish Sea for L.L.Bean’s take, made from Irish-woven lambswool, known for its durability and natural water resistance. Plenty warm and handsome to boot.

Lost & Found’s Scottish lambswool scarf comes with pockets stitched into it. Perfect for stashing your cards, cash or other things a little less above board. We won’t ask.

On the GORP-ier side of things, this thermal fleece scarf balances warmth, stretch and lightweight comfort in a slimmed-down design that will both fit with your puffer and stay out of your way.

Quince has made a name for itself selling luxury materials at un-luxury prices. Case in point: this soft scarf made from 100% Mongolian cashmere, at a price you could get two with.

Another triangle scarf, here in a stunning sienna color that’s still right in Margaret Howell’s wheelhouse. Snug and sensible.

Lil’ brown checks, a fuzzy brushed finish, and Japanese cotton-wool twill woven in England. A big helping of understated charm.

A nice change of pace from the usual winter plaids, two-tone chevrons give this Coach scarf a little graphic punch, while a lightweight but warm alpaca blend keeps things cosy.

If you love pattern, fall and winter is primed for Polo Power. This Fair-Isle-esque design is easier to wear than the classic sweater, and will add some energy to your winter fits.

True to form, Kapital keeps things weird with a wild leopard-and-paisley design. The lightweight gauze also means you can wear it a dozen different ways, pretty much any time of year.

William Lockie’s scarves will set you back a few extra bucks, but they’ve been at it since 1874, so you're buying proven scarf smarts. In this case: Pure cashmere, traditional techniques, and even a pre-sale bath in local fresh water for added softness.

Todd Snyder isn’t reinventing the wheel here, this is just a beautifully brushed cashmere scarf. Classic, timeless, soft, and warm as they come.

Howlin’ often brings a little irreverence to its sweaters, and the same goes for its scarves. Here, throwback collegiate “fun” stripes show the brand’s take on the Ivy scarves of yesteryear.

Made from Italian wool, this Mfpen number gives you two checks for the price of one, thanks to a clever double-faced design. Twist it, drape it, wear it however you please.

All the cozy, old-school charm of an Aran knit, Percival takes the classic cream cable-knit sweater and turns it into a scarf. And at more than half off, it’s a bit of a steal.

She's pricey, but you’re paying for fine Scottish-spun cashmere materials and serious know-how with an entirely handmade and hand-linked scarf.

Printed scarves were the first things Drake’s made back in 1977, when it was still a small workshop. These archival designs are works of art you can wear. Wool, silk and good taste.

Missoni’s famous zigzags came out of swinging ’60s Milan, and they still have that groovy Italian charm. Funny how something so unmistakably of its time never seems to go out of style.

A statement scarf if there ever was one, with vibrant Yves Klein blue and an oversized logo patch that’s not shy about announcing itself. A lot to spend on yourself, maybe, but one hell of a gift.

There’s something dashingly medieval about a shearling scarf. Wrap it around your neck for a bit of Feudal-Lord-core. Beats a suit of armor.

NN07 mixes two old-school patterns into one elegant Italian-woven scarf, with a fuzzy brushed finish and blanket-stitched edges. Your granddad would approve.

This fashion-guy-approved cashmere scarf from Auralee is classic enough, but boy, those rich colours are doing something for me. It truly is all in the details.

By now, you may have noticed the Scots know a thing or two about wool. Johnstons of Elgin has been at it for centuries, and this beautifully woven cashmere scarf is further proof.

#6728. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6727. Culture Watch: What to See and Where to Go in November

Culture Watch is a series spotlighting the intersection of fashion and art, bringing you the latest must-see exhibitions, pop-ups, installations, and more.

November is a good month to make a little room in your calendar. As the holiday season starts to gather pace, galleries, brands, and creative spaces are offering plenty of reasons to get out and look around. In New York, Salon Art + Design returns for its 15th year, while Loro Piana presents its “Master of Cashmere” installation at The Brant Foundation; farther afield, international exhibitions offer even more to explore. Check out all of this month’s best cultural happenings below.

Louis Vuitton Presents ‘La Valise Bruno Aveillan’ at LV Dream

For 13 years, photographer and filmmaker Bruno Aveillan has taken his Louis Vuitton Alzer suitcase to more than 100 destinations, making it a recurring presence in his work. Now, the well-traveled case is at the center of “La Valise Bruno Aveillan,” an immersive exhibition at LV Dream, the house’s encompassing destination in Paris. Aveillan’s photographs appear alongside historic Louis Vuitton trunks and a closer look at the craftsmanship behind the Alzer, the brand’s hard-sided suitcase built around a sturdy wooden frame. The exhibition marks the final chapter in the house’s yearlong celebration of the monogram’s 130th anniversary.

Loro Piana Names Its Cashmere of the Year and Unveils a ‘Master of Cashmere’ Installation

Loro Piana put cashmere in the spotlight at The Brant Foundation in New York, where it marked the 11th edition of its Cashmere of the Year Award. Established in 2015 and held stateside for the first time, the prize recognizes the herders who produce the finest cashmere fiber. Coinciding with the honor, which went to three couples of cashmere herders from Inner Mongolia, is “Master of Cashmere: The Quest for Fiber Excellence,” an installation that traces the material from its origins to the Maison’s work with it. The multi-room experience features archival sketches, explanatory timelines, and, of course, soft-to-the-touch cashmere.

Salon Art + Design Returns to the Park Avenue Armory for Its 15th Year

The 15th edition of Salon Art + Design is now on view at the Park Avenue Armory—and it’s one of its most immersive, expansive editions yet. As is tradition, the event brings together collectible design, fine art, and jewelry. The event is open through November 8. Standouts include Jean Dunand’s 1929 La Forêt lacquered screen, Michel Dufet’s 1918 daybeds, and Jean Royère’s illuminated desk. Fernando Mastrangelo’s totem lamps add a sculptural note, while the jewelry lineup includes pieces from Fernando Jorge, Mellerio, Cora Sheibani, and Viltier.

Lara Saget Debuts Her First New York Solo Show, ‘And the World Came Apart’

Lara Saget brings more than a decade of material experimentation to her first solo exhibition in New York. At Trotter&Sholer’s new Elizabeth Street space, her sculptures and wearable works fuse glass, stone, and metal through heat, pressure, and time. Drawing on geological processes and NASA data, the show moves from ancient natural formations to humanity’s rapid impact on the planet.

The Phillips Collection Opens ‘Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea’

Milton Avery went to Gloucester, Massachusetts, to “live like an artist,” then brought Adolph Gottlieb and Mark Rothko along for summers of creative exchange. In Washington, D.C., The Phillips Collection’s “Avery, Gottlieb & Rothko: By the Sea” brings together watercolors and color-drenched canvases, tracing what those Cape Ann days set in motion.

Tate St Ives Spotlights Wilhelmina Barns-Graham

What does a landscape feel like in the body? Scottish artist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham spent eight decades exploring that question through art shaped by sensation and memory. The retrospective at Tate St Ives in Cornwall, England, is the most comprehensive survey of her work, moving from early landscapes and studio interiors to later works alive with bold color and sweeping gestures.

Taylor Swift, take note: famously hard-to-get-into New York City hotspot The Corner Store has officially landed at The Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas, marking its first-ever location outside Manhattan. Expect its adventurous martinis, signature wood-paneled interiors by Rockwell Group, and a handful of Vegas-exclusive menu additions, including a Butcher’s Counter serving up wagyu tomahawk and porterhouse steaks.

#6726. The Miami Heat Dropped Brand-New Jerseys Just in Time for Grand Theft Auto VI

Growing up in Oakland, Miami Heat forward Keshad Johnson and his brother Kenny used to sneak away from their parents to play Grand Theft Auto. “It caused some fights between me and him on turns,” Johnson says. “We used to play that if you crash the car, you gotta pass the sticks.”

For many of us who came of age in the early aughts, sneaking away from our parents to play GTA was a rite of passage. And since the first edition of the game dropped in 1997, at least part of the thrill of this fictional world was often tied to the clandestine affair. But next week, Johnson won’t be hiding from anybody. Instead, he’ll be part of a once-in-a-lifetime Grand Theft Auto experience when he and his Heat teammates take the court in special-edition Vice City jerseys inspired by the game.

Grand Theft Auto VI, Vice City, launches on November 19th. But the night before, when the Heat and superstar Giannis Antetokounmpo take on his former team, the Milwaukee Bucks, they'll be ringing in what is by most accounts the biggest video game launch of all time with a special event that only Rockstar Games and the Heat could pull off. “My whole family is trying to get a Vice City jersey,” Johnson said when we spoke last weekend.

“We're bringing sports and entertainment together in a way that's never been done,” adds Miami Heat Chief Creative Officer Jennifer Alvarez. “And we're going to deliver an experience that no one has actually had at an NBA game.”

More on that in a second. But let’s start with the kits: all black, with bright pink accents that pop like neon signs in the South Beach sky. The word “Heat” is splashed across the front. “It's kind of like the outlaw type vibe,” Johnson said. “That's what we want to give when we're on the court.”

Hidden inside the letters and jersey numbers is a map of Miami streets. They were designed by Nike and Travis Scott’s Cactus Jack, whose logos are featured on the jersey and shorts. As the whole campaign makes clear, details matter.

“I feel like Vice City has its own fashion culture,” says Heat star Bam Adebayo.

The jerseys will be available for purchase on game night at the arena, where fans will be transported into the video game itself upon entering the Kaseya Center, whose plaza will be made over with a Grotti Cheetah and Albany Manana, just two of the sports cars one can drive in GTA.

A sign hoisted atop the arena will read “Welcome to Vice City.” In fact, Mitchell was late to practice one day because his usual route was blocked by a helicopter that’d been deployed to help install it. “It shows how much time and effort they're trying to put into this new game,” Mitchell says. “This is probably gonna be the greatest game of all time.”

Though everyone involved has kept tight-lipped about what happens once inside the arena, fans attending Heat games have already been able to order burgers from Burger Shot and chicken from Cluckin' Bell, two fictional fast-food chains in the Grand Theft Auto universe. “It's a full 360 experience. I can't wait for people to really understand what that means,” Alvarez said, coyly. “And that's all I can say about it.”

One can understand the secrecy, since the Heat’s Vice City takeover has been two years in the making. It all started when Rockstar Games dropped the trailer for Vice City in December 2023. A digital Kaseya Center can be seen in the first 30 seconds.

“When we saw that we were in the trailer, we thought we should figure something out,” Alvarez recalls. “Because we've been synonymous with the word Vice since 2017."

The Heat launched the Miami Vice campaign in 2017 with its acclaimed Original Vice jerseys that set the standard for NBA teams launching City Edition jerseys. Those campaigns went beyond the uniforms and included local activations like custom license plates and a fashion line created in collaboration with local artists. Over the years, the Heat launched five separate Vice jerseys, each campaign expanding on previous ones. Ask those with the Heat, and they’d agree that this latest installment is the biggest one yet. “It feels like all of it built up to this,” Alvarez said.

To be clear, the Heat don’t look at this as an extension of their own Vice line. Rather, this is meant to be as exclusive as any streetwear brand launch. Also, it’s not easy to transport fans into a video game every single night. Go big, then go home.

Meanwhile, Rockstar has infiltrated Miami, turning the city that inspired Vice City into Vice City itself. Burger Shot came to life through a collaboration with Skinny Louie, a local smash-burger joint that has rebranded their brick-and-mortar (and arena) locations for the launch. Rockstar Games has activations throughout the city, including in Downtown, Little Haiti and the famous Wynwood Walls. It’s an Inception-style, video game outside the video game-type thing that crescendos with the Heat game on the eve of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch.

Players got their first look at the jerseys and the campaign during a team meeting in early October. After hours of presentations about business operations, media responsibilities and other team matters, the energy in the room sparked when Alvarez took the microphone and showed the first Vice City slide. The players locked in. A few even stood up and cheered.

Mitchell, for his part, was taken back to his childhood, when he would come home from his grandma’s house and play Grand Theft Auto until it was time for bed. For a while, Mitchell became obsessed, playing GTA while other popular games like Call of Duty and NBA 2K collected dust.

“I just played that all the time, doing missions, but also just running around,” he remembers. “It's kind of like your own world in a way.”

And next week, he’ll get to enter it IRL.

#6723. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6722. I Own 400 Sneakers. You Should Only Own 21

I own far too many sneakers. There are everyday beaters, rare samples, and plenty in between, accumulated over more than a decade of collecting. That’s a lot of shoes by any reasonable measure. Around 400 at my last count. A few of my favorites took some work to get. I entered a stupid number of raffles for the JJJJound x New Balance 990v3, lined up overnight for the Sacai x Nike VaporWaffle, and caved and paid resale for the Gucci x Adidas Gazelle.

With that many pairs, you start thinking about what actually earns its space. A shoe can be interesting to collect and difficult to wear. Another can seem almost too obvious to buy, then turn out to be the thing that works with most of your clothes. If I could wipe the slate clean, I’d pay much more attention to that second category. I’d still want some fun stuff, obviously. I’m rebuilding a sneaker collection, not writing a packing list.

So, where would I start? With these 21 pairs from Foot Locker’s selection. There are basketball shoes I’d want for their shape and history, runners I’d buy for everyday wear, and a few low-profile pairs to switch things up. Some are famous enough that they barely need an introduction. But knowing a shoe’s name and knowing why you’d want it in your collection are different things. Here’s why these would make it back into mine.

Yes, four of my first five picks are Nike or Jordan – and that’s deliberate. If I were rebuilding my collection, they’d still get a big chunk of my budget. The Air Jordan 1, Air Force 1, and Dunk are a pretty good explanation for why. If you’re starting with jeans and a tee, I’d look here first. A high-top gives you a little more shoe around the ankle. A low-top is easier with shorts, and white Forces can do a lot of the work when you’re getting dressed in a hurry.

I’d start right here, before getting distracted by anything limited to 200 pairs. Peter Moore’s 1985 design gets the shape so right: the height of the collar, the panels around the toe, the way contrasting colors divide up the upper. The High OG also gives you the Nike Air tongue branding. I want a pair that looks good with straightforward jeans and a tee, and the Air Jordan 1 has been perfecting that combo for decades.

A fresh white Air Force 1 would be an early purchase for the deeply boring reason that I’d wear it constantly. Bruce Kilgore’s 1982 basketball silhouette has enough weight to sit properly under loose jeans, and that beefy sole gives the whole fit a little more presence. White-on-white also makes the leather panels and perforations easier to appreciate. It’s the pair I’d reach for when I like everything else I’m wearing and don’t need to complicate things.

Once you’ve looked at enough Dunks, you notice how much the colorblocking changes the sneaker. Its college basketball background gave those panels a specific purpose: carrying team colors. The ‘Sanded Purple’ makes good use of that layout. I’d want a Dunk Low because the shape is uncomplicated enough to wear regularly, while the colors give an outfit a clear starting point. Pick up one of those shades elsewhere, or leave the rest nice and neutral.

The Superstar arrived as a basketball shoe in 1970; Run-D.M.C.’s “My Adidas” helped give it a very different audience in 1986. That history is good to know, but the Shelltoe is what would get my money. It gives the front of the shoe a distinctive shape, and the Superstar II’s extra padding makes the whole thing feel chunkier than the OG. I’d put these under straight jeans, with enough of the toe showing to appreciate it.

The High would come first, of course, but I’d still make room for an Air Jordan 1 Low OG. Removing the tall collar changes how the panels sit with your pants, giving you more space around the ankle and a less bulky-looking sneaker. I’d buy it for days when I want that familiar Jordan colorblocking with shorts or slightly shorter pants. There’s enough difference to justify the second box.

For a day with a lot of walking, I’d start with the 990v6 or the Zoom Vomero 5. There are plenty of ways to get that mesh running-shoe look, and the XT-6 is the one I’d pick if I wanted a trail sole with more grip.

Yes, there would absolutely be gray New Balances in the rebuild. The 990 family started in 1982, but the sixth-gen adds FuelCell cushioning and lets the suede overlays flow across the mesh without the usual midfoot saddle. You can see the difference, and there’s a practical benefit underfoot, too. This is the pair I’d buy for days with a lot of walking: comfy enough to justify the purchase, good-looking enough that comfort isn’t the only justification.

The OG 2008 Gel-Kayano 14 was the first in the series designed by someone other than Toshikazu Kayano – useful information for your next deeply specific sneaker convo. More relevant here is how well the layered mesh and synthetic overlays work together. The ‘Graphite Grey’ has enough contrast to show off the construction, with Gel cushioning right underneath.

The 1906R is for when I want all the little technical details. Open mesh, curvy overlays, and segmented cushioning around the heel give you plenty to check out, especially in white, silver, and black. It shares the same sole tech with the 2002R and 860v2, but the upper just looks more put-together.

The Zoom Vomero 5 launched back in 2011, but it didn’t gain its cult following until about a decade later. There’s a lot to enjoy up top: open mesh, overlapping panels, and plastic caging that becomes particularly obvious in ‘Metallic Silver’. Zoom Air cushioning gives it a practical role in the collection, too. I’d buy this as a regular-wear pair for long days, with enough detail to make jeans and a plain sweater look put together.

First released in 2010, the Omni 9 has all the mesh and supporting structure you’d expect from a running shoe of that era. This white and pink version lets you see how the layers fit together, with ProGrid cushioning underneath. I’d want it because a collection can become very repetitive once you find a couple of brands you like. The Omni gives me another interpretation of the technical runner, with enough character to earn its place alongside the Nikes and Asics.

The P-6000 looks like a straight archive reissue, but it actually combines elements from the Pegasus 25 and Pegasus 2006. I’d buy the white and silver combo and wear the hell out of them – every pair doesn’t need to be an occasion.

The XT-6 started life in 2013 as a serious trail running shoe, and you can still see that purpose in the reinforced upper, Quicklace system, and lugged outsole. My plans would probably involve considerably less altitude. I’d buy it because the close-fitting upper and outdoor construction bring something different to the collection, particularly with cargo pants or wider-leg pants. The ‘Black Coffee’ also makes it easy to wear with denim, olive, and navy. No hiking itinerary required.

If your jeans taper or you like a shorter hem, try something that sits closer to the foot. The Samba is an easy place to start in black leather. I’d go for the green Spezial if I wanted a little color without having to think too hard about the rest of the fit.

Collecting can make you weird about buying something that everybody else owns – I’d try to avoid that with the Samba. Its roots go back to soccer shoes for icy fields in 1950, but the slim shape is what earns it a place here. After a few chunky basketball shoes, you need something that sits closer to the foot. ‘Core Black’ leather, white stripes, and a suede T-toe give you plenty to work with, particularly under a straighter pair of pants.

Yes, there’s already a Samba here. The Handball Spezial earns its own place with its rounded toe, suede upper, and gum sole, which give it a softer appearance than the leather-heavy pairs. First made for handball players in 1979, it’s also a good way to bring some color into the rebuild. The green and white do enough on their own. I’d wear these with blue jeans and let the suede take care of the rest.

The Gazelle dates back to 1966, making this year its 60th birthday. I’d buy it for the suede upper and the straightforward proportions, which give it a slightly different feel from the other Adidas silhouettes here. In black and white, it’s easy to wear with faded denim or dark pants. Some days, a familiar shape in simple colors is exactly what you want.

Puma’s Suede history runs back to 1968, so I’d want some of that history in the collection, as well as the shoe’s simple construction. The soft upper and sweeping Formstrip give you texture and shape without a bunch of extra panels. It would be a useful change after several technical runners, especially with denim or cotton pants that already have plenty of texture themselves.

Wide jeans and heavier layers can take a bigger shoe. I’d look at the Air Max 95 for the layered upper, the Gel-NYC if I wanted something a little quieter, or the 9060 if I wanted the sole to do most of the talking.

Sergio Lozano was inspired by human anatomy for the Air Max 95, translating ribs, muscle fibers, and a spine into a running shoe. A pretty weird design concept that produced a very good sneaker. Those layered side panels are the reason I’d buy it again: they give the shoe depth even in this low-key black, white, and gray combination. It has enough bulk for wider pants, and enough going on that the rest of the fit can stay simple.

The Gel-NYC looks pretty old school, but Asics actually assembled it from several archive references. There’s Gel-Nimbus 3 and Gel-MC Plus V in the upper, with Gel-Cumulus 16 tooling underneath. The result has a fuller shape than the Kayano, with more emphasis on those broad suede panels. That’s why I’d make room for both. This ‘Cream’ and ‘Oyster Grey’ version works particularly well beneath wider pants, where a very slim shoe can disappear under the hem.

A collection of completely sensible sneakers would feel like an opportunity missed. The 9060 takes details from New Balance’s 99X family and blows them up: the 990’s sway bars spread across the upper, while the sole gets a sculpted, pod-like shape. I’d pick this brown version to balance out bigger pants and heavier layers. It gives those clothes a chunky enough shoe to sit over.

These are the two I’d happily get dirty. Go for the Chucks if you like a high-top with cuffed jeans, or the Old Skools if you want something low that’s just as easy to wear with shorts.

Black canvas Chucks would be back on the shelf pretty quickly, too. Their basketball DNA stretches all the way back to 1917, but it’s the narrow shape I’d want in this collection. It gives jeans a completely different finish from an AF1 or a 990, especially with a little ankle showing. These are also shoes I’d be happy to wear until the canvas softened and the rubber picked up some marks.

To finish off my new collection, I’d grab a pair of Old Skools. Launched in 1977 as the Style 36, it introduced the Jazz Stripe along the way. The canvas-and-suede upper, white stripe, and waffle sole are still enough to make it worth owning. It looks good with jeans, works with shorts, and improves once the upper loosens up. After all the comparing and researching and rebuilding, I’d want at least one pair I could put on and forget about.

#6719. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6717. The Secret to Kendall Jenner’s ‘Me Mode’

The model and founder shares her favorite ways to unwind and how the Therabody TheraFace Mask Glo fits into her nightly routine.

For Kendall Jenner, “Me Mode” is a time to unplug from the daily demands of work and social obligations and simply be still. “I have a really busy mind, so switching off has never come naturally to me,” says the model and entrepreneur. “I’ve had to build little rituals that help me slow down.”

One of those rituals involves Therabody’s TheraFace Mask Glo, an LED face mask that bridges skincare with wellness. Delivering full LED coverage across the entire face, including the lips and under eyes, the cordless device features 504 red, infrared, and blue LEDs, plus a relaxing scalp massage to help relieve tension. Best of all, treatment time is only 12 minutes, giving Jenner a quick, easy, and much-needed pause from her busy schedule.

“After a long day, it’s sweatpants, my dogs, and zero plans,” Jenner says. “Putting on the Mask Glo has kind of become my signal that the day is over. For those 12 minutes, my brain finally goes quiet.”

One thing Jenner loves about the TheraFace Mask Glo is how effortlessly it fits into her routine. “It’s hands-free, so I just put it on and do whatever I feel like that night,” Jenner says. “Sometimes that’s music or journaling, and a lot of the time it’s doing absolutely nothing. The scalp massage is my favorite part. It feels less like a skincare step and more like actually relaxing.”

It offers legitimate skincare benefits, too. Backed by the largest clinical study of any LED mask on the market, the TheraFace Mask Glo was shown to reduce under-eye wrinkles and fine lines, enhance radiance, and lift sagging skin in as little as eight weeks.

The TheraFace Mask Glo offers three LED settings to target different skin concerns. Red light helps improve the appearance of fine lines, wrinkles, and dark spots, while red and infrared light work together to boost collagen production. Blue light targets acne-causing bacteria, helping prevent future breakouts.

The key is consistent use, which Jenner has found easy to maintain. “If a routine is too complicated, I’m not going to stick with it, and I’ve learned that consistency matters more than anything,” she says. “With the Mask Glo, I pick red, red and infrared, or blue light depending on how my skin is acting, and that’s it. It’s easy enough that I actually use it, which is half the battle for me. It comes with me when I travel now, too.”

The LED lights are placed across the entire face, even covering overlooked areas like the mouth and eyes. The preset treatment runs for 12 minutes, cycling through four minutes of each light setting. Four-minute individual treatments are also available.

Combining advanced skincare and relaxation into one simple step, the TheraFace Mask Glo is ideal for anyone who wants to level up their nighttime routine with minimal effort. As Jenner has learned over the years, less is more when it comes to beauty and wellness.

“I’ve been sitting in makeup chairs since I was 14, so I went through a phase of trying everything,” she says. “Now I do a lot less, and I’m more intentional about what I put on my skin. I try to give it a break when I can, and I’ll use the Mask Glo before glam on shoot days.”

Jenner’s nighttime routine is just one aspect in living a more holistic lifestyle. “Wellness for me is mostly about balance now: being at the barn with my horses, getting outside, and protecting my nights,” she says. “My friends make fun of me for going to bed so early, but I’m not changing.”
