#6692. The Minimalist ’90s-Style Coat Will Be Everywhere This Winter

The return of ’90s fashion is hardly new territory for the Vogue Shopping desk. But if 2026 has proved anything, it’s that our collective obsession with the decade isn’t going anywhere anytime soon. This year, Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy fever swept the headlines for months, coinciding with the release of Ryan Murphy’s hit drama Love Story, which (albeit after a few costume department consultations) sparked a return to the late fashion icon’s off-duty photographs, in search of styling inspiration.

“The online deluge of CBK content isn’t just generating likes; it’s been driving sales, too—a quick browse of the websites of Massimo Dutti or Reformation will give you some idea of just how swiftly brands have moved to capitalize on consumer fascination with this uncomplicated, clean aesthetic,” wrote Vogue’s Emma Spedding in her recent story on minimalism’s continued grip on our autumn wardrobes. She outlined the single-breasted longline coat as a key piece in achieving the sought-after CBK look–alongside a pencil skirt, turtleneck vest and simple leather bag.

Such coats were a cornerstone of the ’90s collections of Calvin Klein, Jil Sander, and Helmut Lang, characterised by (but not bound to) clean lines, understated single-breasted buttoning, discreet masculine lapels and a long, lean silhouette. Usually rendered in a palette of black, charcoal grey, beige, camel, and chocolate brown.

CBK was frequently photographed on the streets of New York in versions crafted from both wool and lighter-weight gabardine, styled off-duty with straight-leg jeans, oval sunglasses and an Alice band by day, or draped over a simple LBD (probably Calvin Klein) with pointed black slingbacks (probably Prada) into the night. Kate Moss, too, favored the style in her early Soho days, often opting for a cashmere camel iteration.

For fall/winter 2026, the coat shape was a key style on the runway. Jil Sander, unsurprisingly, remains something of an authority on the subject, offering a multitude of interpretations, from extra-long and oversized to collarless and polished leather styles. Elsewhere, designers have found ways to disrupt the coat’s pared-back credentials. Dries Van Noten introduced a satin finish and statement pixelated graphic, while Miu Miu did what Miu Miu does best and took the familiar shape, rendered it in crumpled leather and added a fuzzy faux-fur trim.

Unlike more statement-making outerwear that often dominates the discourse, a well-cut, single-breasted coat does a lot with very little, whether layered over tailoring for the office, worn with jeans and loafers at the weekend or thrown over eveningwear as the nights draw in.

Look for a shape that falls below the knee, a relatively clean shoulder line and enough room to accommodate a knit underneath, without swamping you when worn with bare arms. Of course, wool and cashmere styles will earn their keep on colder days, but lighter cotton versions make a useful option for milder weather and transitional dressing.

The long-line ’90s coat makes a convincing case for buying less, but buying well. Scroll on to discover our edit of the best minimalist coats to shop now.

#6687. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6685. The Scoop with RBO’s Sophie Wybrew-Bond: On Their Festive Partnership with L’Oréal

Welcome to the Scoop: a weekly email series in which I quiz fashion insiders on the stories of the week. This will be a way for the Vogue Business community to synthesize and reflect on the latest headlines and get a little inside scoop every Friday.

This week’s guest is the Royal Ballet and Opera’s chief commercial officer, Sophie Wybrew-Bond. After a career in media, Sophie joined the Royal Opera House in 2024, as the organization looked to build a more resilient mixed-funding model.

One of the first things Sophie did was to add the word ‘ballet’ to the name. Ballet is half of what the company does, but according to Sophie, 30% of their audience didn’t know it. They do now — and they have grown as well. In the years since Covid, the RBO’s social channels have grown from about 3 million followers to 7.5 million, mostly because they began posting content that felt light and organic, rather than branded.

At the same time, much like everywhere else in culture, brand partners at the Royal Ballet and Opera House are arguably more important than ever. I called up Sophie to find out their plans for the festive season.

This year’s festive partner for the Royal Ballet and Opera is L’Oréal. This is the second time we have had a Christmas partner — last year’s was Paul Smith. L’Oréal is designing the Christmas tree in the Paul Hamlyn Hall. The concept we are working with is “Where beauty meets performance”.

We want a tree of discovery; meaning that people come into the house and even if they don’t have a ticket, they’ll spend a bit of time looking and finding details and delightful extra bits that you don’t notice at first glance. We’ve got 10 bespoke dioramas, which are like little storytelling elements to the tree, which then have L’Oréal products within them. At the top of the tree, we’ve got a star made of pointe shoes that glitter. We will be unveiling the tree next Wednesday, November 18.

We actually also announced a beauty partnership with L’Oréal just recently, which means their product is being used by our wigs, hair and makeup teams. One of our principals, Marianela Nunez, who’s been with the company for 26 years, is the face of that partnership. As part of that, we offer some behind-the-scenes tours to our community. We program moments during the holidays, where you can drink and dine or listen to music — and it will be all around the tree. Because of The Nutcracker, people will be coming into the house to feel festive.

Christmas tree ornaments composed of L’Oréal products.

How did the partnership with L’Oréal happen?

It’s really important for us that partnerships are not like a badge-type sponsorship. The storytelling on digital channels is as important. While thousands of people will see this tree, hundreds of thousands more will see it on digital channels across the world. The impact that we had with our Paul Smith partnership last year was pretty visible so L’Oréal came to us to explore working together.

I was interviewing Sydney Levrone last week at the Vogue Business Global Summit. She spoke about the relationship between sport and beauty, and how all the track and field athletes these days are “completely glammed out”.

Certainly, the Royal Ballet dancers are elite athletes and then they need to have an artistic interpretation on top of the technique and the athleticism they exhibit. It sets the bar really high on both sides. So when it comes to beauty, you need to make sure you have a partner who meets those standards with high performance products. The product needs to last through really extreme circumstances, which is why we came up with that “beauty meets performance” theme.

Behind the scenes for the festive preparations at Royal Ballet & Opera.

How closely do you follow fashion? And why is it important for ballet to be connected to the fashion and luxury industries?

In our case, we’re very, very interested in how fashion houses are telling their stories. But fashion and ballet have always been quite closely connected. Obviously, costumes have to be aesthetically beautiful, but they also have to perform. They have to work with choreography, they have to allow movement and breathing, but also hold their shape in this high-performance environment. As fashion has had such an evolution in terms of textile and cut and the way things move, it’s easy to see the common threads all the way through.

We have worked with so many brands and designers, including Erdem, Daniel Lee at Burberry, Roksanda, Saul Nash and Gareth Pugh.

It’s been almost a year since Timothée Chalamet said no one cares about ballet and opera any more. Yet, as we reported, we have seen a tremendous interest on fashion’s side for ballet this year. Is there a connection between the two — did the comments lead to a renewed interest in ballet?

Not at all. There is a news cycle which obviously has peaks and troughs. And then there is perennial shared storytelling. I think what happened with those comments is that they spiked in the news cycle at that point in time, but the relationship between fashion and ballet is always there. Timothée Chalamet’s comments provoked a reaction and so kickstarted a news cycle, which we were able to use for more storytelling on social media and the overwhelming positive response was just brilliant.

Podcasts are having a moment. Do you guys have one?

Right now, we’re in the cinema, on socials and on YouTube. I want us to be part of whatever the conversation is, and to do that we need to be on channels and in formats where people aren’t expecting to see us. It’s not about selling tickets but about having the Royal Ballet and Opera perceived as exciting and relevant, even if they are only following us on social media. I am developing some audio products. Watch this space. There’ll be another scoop.

#6684. Best Men’s Winter Parkas 2026: 17 Heavy-Duty Snow-Busting Coats

The best men's parka is a lot like an upright sleeping bag, except it doesn't simply keep you insulated. It also protects your frostbite-prone fits from Mother Nature’s icy clutches, and keeps you looking sharp in the process. Don't believe us? Just ask the parka's most loyal servant: Oasis frontman Liam Gallagher.

Before giving you our favourites, some quick history: Parkas originated in the Arctic, where the Inuit designed them to withstand bone-chilling temperatures. They then made their way to the US military with the introduction of the N-3B parka in the 1950s. Throughout its evolution, the parka's mission has remained unchanged: to keep not just your torso warm, but your thighs and rear end too. Seriously, you've already worn that waist-length puffer to death: Make like Justin Jefferson. Go long.

The North Face McMurdo down parka isn’t just another winter coat—it’s a cold-weather icon with Antarctic-level credibility. Named after McMurdo Station, the US research hub in Antarctica, this parka is designed to thrive in below-freezing temperatures while keeping you comfortable and protected. With 600-fill recycled down insulation and windproof, waterproof, and breathable DryVent technology, it’s eco-friendly armor for the tundra—or the Target parking lot. Made from recycled nylon and polyester, it’s part of The North Face’s recycled-repurpose collection, combining sustainability with serious performance.

Loaded with features like six exterior pockets, a removable faux-fur ruff, an adjustable hood, and a draft flap, this 3.5-pound powerhouse is your portable fortress of warmth. Stylish touches like the midnight petrol color elevate it above standard winter fare, while practical details make it indispensable for everything from scraping windshields to tackling arctic adventures. Whether you’re braving brutal weather or commuting in comfort, the McMurdo is built to last—complete with The North Face’s warranty to keep it in the game longer than your ever-disappearing gloves.

Mountain Hardwear has been a staple in the outdoor gear world long before its sold-out collaboration with Stüssy (though they’ve probably gained a few new fans in the process). Founded in 1993 in Richmond, California, the brand spun off from the well-known outdoor company Sierra Designs. A group of designers and engineers left Sierra Designs to create Mountain Hardwear, and 32 years later, it’s still famous for its technical outerwear, sleeping bags, and pioneering use of Gore-Tex.

This jacket is built for camping, featuring a durable ripstop shell and 650-fill down. With a fully adjustable insulated hood and a drawcord at the waist to trap in heat, it’s tough to top even before you encounter the two BYO-bevvy pockets—specially designed to carry your favorite beverages. Whether you're in your tent or Air Streamer, this jacket keeps you warm—and your drinks cold—so you can stay cozy and hydrated in style.

Woolrich: So good it doesn't need a logo patch. The American outdoor company was founded in 1830, and since then has become the destination for warmth-minded men who don't need anyone else to know they're walking around in the very best materials.

Which isn't to say this parka won't turn some heads. New for this season, it comes in seven colors, from a stunning light blue to nutty falcon brown, and also boasts some envy-inducing hand-warmer pockets, hidden rib-knit cuffs, and even a water-repellent finish. (A nice touch for a style that typically is more preoccupied with keeping out the cold than the wet.) One more thing: It's called the Cloud because it's incredibly light, even with a 90/10 duck down fill. A winter coat that wears like a summer-weight hoodie? Worth the investment.

This is the kind of Canada Goose jacket that reminds you why the brand is so much more than just a status symbol for finance guys. (Though I'm sure they don't mind being that too.) For one, it's done away with that ubiquitous blue and red logo, and replaced it with a more understated, tonal patch. But that's actually the only thing that's been stripped back here: Otherwise, this parka is packed full of features, from ribbed knit cuffs, to pockets everywhere you look, to a bevy of insulation considerations, from the 625 Fill Down interior all the way to the soft, lined chin guard—a nice touch.

Available this season in Black, Olive, and Desert Sand (above), it's backed by Canada Goose's lifetime guarantee. So, yes, you're spending a fortune. But the brand stands ready to make sure you'll never need to buy another parka again.

The Japanese label FrizmWORKS has reimagined a classic, ‘60s‐era expedition parka silhouette—quilted down, hard-wearing cotton-blend shell, boxy hooded cut—and, sixty years later, given it a whole new life. From the tonal matte finish to the utilitarian drawcord hem, this is a mountain‐camp relic reimagined for your 2025 commute. It’s rugged without resorting to SSX Tricky branding, and along with the requisite down filling also has two fun, unexpected and large pockets on the back. It also comes in a joyful orange color, if that black is a little too subtle for you.

I can't be the only one who was excited to see Reigning Champ get back into making real clothes. (Though, let’s be honest, the brand’s sweatsuits are still some of my favorites.) But this high-powered, goose-filled nylon parka? It's built for Canadian winters, which means it’ll easily thrive anywhere else, too. Technically, that means 700 fill power down, and a weather-repellent nylon shell to keep out wind and rain, as well as the colder temps. Its defining feature is its stealthy, all-black appearance, and Reigning Champ has leant hard into that vibe, with hidden interior pockets, concealed rib cuffs, and a shock cord hood that you can pull as tight as you like. Now you see me, now you don't.

The new kids on the parka block, Big Rock Candy Mountaineering, are bringing the fun back with their vibrant, winter parka colors. These extreme cold-weather parkas take inspiration from mid-century American outdoor brands. Can’t think of any off the top of your head? Skim through a book like this, and you’ll catch the vibe.

BRCM’s parkas are packed with cozy duck down and feature a 100% grosgrain shell. This ribbed texture, courtesy of its tight weave, makes the fabric tough as nails and resistant to wear and tear. The ginormous pockets? Perfect for stashing your winter accessories (or your snacks). And if the wind has you feeling like it’s got something to prove, just tighten up the drawstring waist, hood, and hem. One of the coolest features? The jacket’s silhouette. When cinched, you can clasp your bag around the waist—ideal for those who love a good backpacking adventure. Although BRCM is still a fresh face in the outerwear world, it already feels like an instant classic.

Getting your hands on one of the first-ever parkas is basically impossible—right up there with finding your keys when you’re already late. Enter The Real McCoy’s, which somehow pulls it off with museum-grade reproductions. Every detail is obsessively dialed, down to the DuPont-developed nylon shell that helped kick off the whole modern-materials era.

Today’s outdoor companies are still trying to capture Patagonia’s lightning-in-a-bottle formula from when the brand first burst onto the scene: Be nice to everyone, make products the right way, and design jackets built to last forever. Take its Glacier parka, for example: it’s weatherproof, cozy enough to double as a sleeping bag, and so comfortable you might consider skipping the tent altogether.

If you’re after a quieter, minimalist parka—and you’ve got the budget—the Therme Parka delivers. It’s hip-length, packed with goose down, and built with the brand’s more environmentally friendly GORE-TEX ePE fabric, meaning it’s primed to handle a lifetime of winters.

The Alpha Industries N-3B is the real-deal snorkel parka—because it is the real deal. Produced early in the company's history in the 1950s, the parka is still tough as nails and loaded with reinforced elbow patches, a full-length storm flap, and snug inset knit cuffs that keep wind firmly in its place.

Founded in 1960, Fjällräven are sort of Sweden's Patagonia. By which we mean they've always thought about three things: High-performance materials, a reasonable enough price point, and dressing it all up in some great primary colors.

Nanga is your favorite outerwear brand’s favorite outerwear brand. Its parka riffs on the US Air Force’s N-3B flight jacket, upgraded with AuroraTex—a high-performance fabric that keeps you dry no matter what. Add handwarmer pockets and a discreet cigar pouch, and you’ve got a parka that nails the perfect blend between utility and style.

Goldwin is so good, it literally owns the North Face in Japan. (Like, literally.) This handsome down parka is wind-blocking, body-warming, and equipped with a PERTEX Quantum ripstop lining (and shell) to prevent the tears and rips that lightweight fabrics can otherwise be prone to.

Berghaus' Meru jacket—which is long enough to qualify as a parka in our book—is packed with retro styling, from the color blocks to the cinchable waistband. 2L Gore-Tex means you could wear it up any peak, but its general aura means you could also wear it up on stage, hands behind your back, tambourine on your head.

Montbell's mastery of lightweight, easy-to-rock, nicely-priced outdoors gear has become its calling card, and it’s on full display here. This down parka is easy to incorporate into pretty much any wardrobe, and even has some nice-looking stitching (which, by the way, the heads call ‘baffling’).

What do you get when you cross a parka with a fireman jacket? A full-scale compliment magnet.

First and foremost: functionality. A great parka should incorporate more features than a midnight infomercial. In the outer shell, you’ll typically find materials like nylon or polyester, and sometimes more rugged options like Gore-Tex. But it's also worth peeking under the hood—literally. Parkas are usually filled with down (duck or goose feathers) or synthetic insulation like polyester. Down is warm and lightweight, but it’s the fair-weather friend of insulation—it falters when wet. Synthetic insulations, on the other hand, is the ride-or-die option, keeping you warm even when soggy.

Hoods are another essential feature. Most will be made of a weatherproof fabric, and some come equipped with fluffy genuine- or faux-fur trims that gently tickle your face with a touch of winter luxury. And then there are the pockets—no one wants to walk around in a blizzard with frozen fingers. (Look for fleece linings.) Finally, asses the length. Longer parkas offer more warmth and protection from the elements, while shorter ones are perfect for commuters who need to dodge frostbite without overheating on the subway.

While function is the defining characteristic of a good parka, a great one should also give your winter fits a serious upgrade. Pair it with a thermal and a chunky sweater for a no-brainer look, or go bold by layering it over a denim jacket, adding corduroys, and anchoring with sturdy boots.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6683. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6682. Daisy Edgar-Jones’s Favorite Smart-Crop Jeans Are the Fall Denim Trend to Try Now

Known for her love of vintage Levi’s, the actor has shown no signs of abandoning her trusty denim.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In recent years, press tours have become even buzzier than whatever’s being promoted. Not that we’re complaining—we were first in line to gush over the array of bright pink outfits Margot Robbie wore throughout her 2023 press appearances for Barbie, and again earlier this year when the actor was promoting Wuthering Heights, gracing our social feeds with enviable corsetry reminiscent of her character, Cathy.

As for another scene-stealing star who knows how to turn a look, Daisy Edgar-Jones has been out in force in a mixture of casual and formal outfits to promote her latest on-screen endeavor, Sense and Sensibility. Styled by Dani Michelle, Edgar-Jones has been on a run of wearing some of the most buzzy luxury labels, including Prada, Chloé, and Schiaparelli.

But this time, it’s not the statement pieces we’ve got our eye on. Instead, a humble pair of jeans.

Known for her love of vintage Levi’s, Edgar-Jones has been photographed wearing the same pair of straight, cropped jeans on two occasions during this ongoing press tour. Styling them on the first outing with an archive Galliano top with a cinched waist and blossoming collar, she finished the look with a Boucheron choker and gold peep-toe heels. The rigid, straight denim, although more casual than a tailored trouser, worked well to keep the look feeling elevated, without leaning into something overly formal. Likewise, the cropped leg gave the shoes a much-deserved moment in the spotlight.

For the second look of the day, the star simply swapped out her top and shoes, opting for a strapless corset and nude pumps. Here, the jeans added a relaxed edge to the feminine ensemble, allowing just a little ankle to show at the hem. Where other trending styles such as barrel-legs and wide jeans are great for everyday, Edgar-Jones proves that a pair of straight, cropped jeans is a smart alternative for when the dress code reads “elevated-casual.”

#6681. The Comfy Pants BA Editors Are Wearing to Thanksgiving

Thanksgiving is my favorite holiday, not an uncommon feeling around the BA offices. I love the planning, the days (yes: days plural) spent preparing the feast in the kitchen alongside my mom, the gathering of loved ones around a table to reflect, savor, and enjoy. There is one thing, however, that I don’t love: The moment after dinner and before dessert in which I become so full that I must excuse myself and retire to the couch, where I clutch a pillow to my stomach until I’ve digested enough to reemerge.

As somewhat of an expert in feeling Too Full and Bloated™, I can attest that this feeling is made infinitely worse when I’m wearing rigid, tight-waisted pants. Perhaps you can relate? While stretchy sweatpants are an obvious solution here, there are only so many meal scenarios in which it’s socially acceptable to wear them. For those other occasions—the holiday feasts, celebratory meals out, and thousand-course tasting menu dinners—I’ve made it my mission to fill my wardrobe with pants that look polished and feel comfortable, no matter how many helpings of stuffing or “fries for the table” I’ve had. Here are my tried-and-true favorite pairs for eating big meals in, along with my fellow food-loving colleagues’ go-tos.

I was a die-hard high-waist pants gal for the majority of my life. Then I tried Still Here’s Everyday Jeans. A true mid-rise, they hit just above my hip bones and about an inch below my belly button, hugging my body without digging in, even after a holiday dinner or multicourse restaurant meal. The non-stretch denim is soft but sturdy, and the relaxed leg is structured without feeling at all rigid. I own them in Washed Black and Classic Blue and wear them constantly, to everything from casual weeknight dinners (paired with sneakers and a white tee) to weekend date nights (with kitten heels and a silk top). They’ve even become my go-to Friendsgiving uniform in recent years because of how comfortable they are to cook, eat, and host in.

If you haven’t already heard of Rag & Bone’s Miramar line, let me put you on: These pants look like real denim, but are actually made from soft cotton terry. It’s all thanks to the brand’s printing technique, which allows them to digitally print details like weave, stitching, buttons, and pockets onto any fabric. Ever since I got my first pair, I’ve been delighted every time I receive a compliment on my jeans and can reveal that they’re actually—gasp—sweatpants! I’ve owned the Sofie style for a few years now, which have real pockets and a true button fly that give them a more polished look; but my recent obsession are the Sport Stripe Track Pants, which have a flattering wide-leg cut and a fully elastic waistband that makes them ideal for multicourse meals.

I invested in a pair of poplin pants from Suzie Kondi this summer and they’ve quickly become my go-to attire whenever I want the comfort of an elastic waistband while still looking put-together. The low-rise waist sits comfortably on my hips and ensures that nothing squeezes my midsection, and the straight leg cut is incredibly flattering. The cotton poplin fabric is breathable and feels quite luxe, and I’ve even noticed that stains come out surprisingly easily (which I learned the hard way by spilling green juice all over myself testing personal blenders). Forever a fan of a monochrome ’fit, I love pairing mine with the matching Vella shirt.

If you’re looking for a more affordable option, J.Crew’s Luna Pants have gained a well-deserved following on social media this year. They’re just as stylish as the pricier brands, available in several colors, and ring in at under $100.

Many of the above pants feel like sweatpants, but if you’re enjoying a casual dinner, there’s nothing stopping you from wearing actual sweatpants—particularly if you opt for an elevated pair that ditches the typical brushed fleece for cashmere or velour in a straight-leg cut. Senior reviews editor Olivia Tarantino and I are both fans of Quince’s Mongolian Cashmere Straight Leg Pants for their ultrasoft feel and flattering cut. If you’re looking to upgrade to something more luxe, executive audience development director Casey Hendricks vouches for the cashmere Everywhere Pant from Guest in Residence: “They’re THE pants for when you can’t fathom wearing actual pants. They’re comfortable but structured for sweatpants, and they’re super warm. I’ve had these pants for years and they still feel and look good as new.” I’m also partial to Suzie Kondi’s Lito Pants, which are cut from cozy velour and have a slightly flared leg that looks good on everyone. While I don’t own these myself, I steal my mom’s pair every time I’m home to visit (sorry, Mom!).

100% Washable Silk Drawstring Wide Leg Pants

For dressier dinners, I like to opt for a pair of slinky satin pants. The elastic waistband and flowy fabric ensures they stay comfy even after the meal is said and done, while the shine and elegant drape make them easy to dress up. Hendricks calls La Ligne’s Colby Pants her “everything pants.” She says she wears them for “work, errands, eating, airport, and everything in between. They’re so comfortable but also so chic—they make me feel effortlessly put-together.” I also love Quince’s 100% Washable Silk Drawstring Wide Leg Pants, which have an impressive sub-$100 price tag and are (as the name suggests) magically machine washable.

Long gone are the days where I’ve been an athleisure-on-the-plane kind of girl. In this job (and in life in general), I've started to prefer clothes that are both comfortable and acceptable to wear to a restaurant meal straight from the plane. Enter the Reformation Olina Linen Pants. They’re perhaps the only pants that I’d wear on an 11-hour travel day straight into a few-hours-long dinner, and in fact, I have. The linen gives them an elevated look, but the drawstring waist and just-soft-enough fabric make them easy to sit in for a long while. I’m tempted to order them in every color, but my singular pair has lasted many trips, many meals, and many washes thus far. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager

As an adult man approaching 40, I want a pair of pants just wide enough to convey I’m in the know without going full MC Hammer. Enter the Uniqlo pleated, relaxed wide pants. With an elastic, drawstring waistband and belt loops, I get to dine out free from navel constrictions and still wear a smart belt. I can go from the office to the bistro to the couch without sacrificing comfort or functionality. To you, the casual observer, though, I look like I’m wearing slacks. With the loose, high-waist fit, these pants drape beautifully with a pair of black leather penny loafers. They’re made of 67% recycled polyester, which feels virtuous and breezy. —Gabe Hiatt, senior restaurants editor

I am content with my daily uniform of selvedge jeans, leather shoes, and a dark T-shirt or sweater depending on the weather. It’s not too formal for working in a kitchen, but acceptable should I find myself in an elevator with someone from Vogue. But running around town all day, with the occasional epic dinner out, means a constant trade-off between style and comfort. Whoever designed 100% cotton jeans for railroad workers and miners just didn’t consider the rigors of a 3-hour meal followed by a long train ride home. So lately I have been quietly upgrading my look with Naked and Famous Denim’s stretch selvedge jeans. They contain 2% elastane (perhaps you know it as Spandex), just enough to provide a forgiving fit, but with the look and patina of raw denim. They stay conformable enough all day that you can simply ignore them and think about more important things: like dinner. —Chris Morocco, food director

There is no worse feeling than the cold, hard button of a stiff jean pressing against your full stomach after a particularly big meal. (Who designed jeans anyway?). That’s why for Thanksgiving there won’t be a firm, oppressive waistband in sight. I already know I’ll be donning my Le Bon Shoppe Arc Pants, not only for their loose barrel-leg silhouette, but also for their forgiving elasticated waist band. Namely, more pie for me, without the feeling of “pants” up against my indulgent belly. Pair with a festive cashmere sweater (preferably oversized) and you can go from the dinner table straight to the couch for your turkey-induced coma in both style and comfort. —June Kim, executive editor

As someone who’s no stranger to a mid-meal top-button release, I’ve developed a deep appreciation for an elastic waistband. Even better when it comes in a pair of pants I’m excited to wear. My current favorite: J.Crew’s Luna pants in lightweight corduroy. A more fall-friendly take on the poplin version above, these are like sweatpants disguised as corduroys, with plenty of room for big Thanksgiving ambitions while still making you feel put-together. Honestly, what more could you ask of a pant?

You can dress them up with a sweater and loafers or keep it casual with a T-shirt and sneakers. I’ve worn them so often that I’m already plotting a second pair in a different color. My one caveat: They tend to run a little big, so I’d suggest sizing down. —Gabby Fowler, social media director

#6680. My First Job in Fashion: Renzo Rosso

This story is part of 'My First Job in Fashion', interviews with fashion insiders on the roles who made them who they are today.

My first ever job outside my family’s farm was as a carpenter. Every summer, from the age of 10 until I was 16, I worked for a woodworking company that made kitchen furniture. One summer, they put me with two guys building a dining table — one of those extendable ones where you add a leaf in the middle. Every day I went to work and did exactly the same thing: I was the kid helping two men put together the same table, over and over again.

Within a month, the owner had moved the other two onto a different project and left me to make the tables by myself.

A young Renzo Rosso with his father, Vittorio, and mother Fortunata.

I’ve always had a slightly different way of working; I think a little differently from most people. But I love being part of a team, and I have always looked for people who know the things I don’t. That’s how I worked with John Galliano, for instance. I am not a designer — he is. But we were always in conversation, and together we made Maison Margiela a real success.

I grew up in Brugine, in the countryside not far from Venice, Italy. My parents were farmers, and they wanted at least one of their three children to study. My father decided it should be me. For secondary school, I chose the textile program at the Marconi Technical Institute in Padua — a fashion school — because it was the easiest. I didn’t like studying.

But I loved jeans. Growing up, I wore my brother’s hand-me-downs. Then one day, when I was 12, I saw a pair of jeans at the market and begged my mother to please, please buy them for me. She did, that same day. I felt like a king at school; all the kids admired those jeans. I loved them so much I never took the paper tag off the back pocket. I just wore them to school with the tag on. Something inside me was already calling me to fashion. I just didn’t know it yet.

It was the early 1970s, and you have to understand what that time was like. Kids were really starting to rebel against their parents’ generation. It was the Beatles and the Rolling Stones, marijuana, people throwing away their suits for denim. It was a revolution.

At Marconi, I made my first pair of jeans: low-rise and flared. Then I made more on my mother’s sewing machine and sold them to my friends. That’s also when I had the idea of stone-washing. The denim felt too stiff, so I took a stone and started rubbing the jeans with it to soften them.

Fashion school gave me structure. It taught me patterns, stitching, and how the industry works. But I am not a designer; I am someone with good ideas. I went on to study economics at Ca' Foscari, the University of Venice, but I dropped out in 1976 to take my first real job in fashion.

A friend told me about an opening at a clothing manufacturer called Moltex. I went in for an interview with the owner, Adriano Goldschmied, and told him two things: that I was qualified for the job, and that I had already done my military service, which was mandatory in Italy at the time. Neither was true. I had never worked in fashion, and I was still waiting for my call-up letter. Thank God, it never came.

Adriano hired me as production manager at Moltex, which made trousers for one of his brands, Daily Blue. There were 20 girls working there and huge stacks of denim to get through every day. Luckily, I learn fast. Unluckily, I also liked to party — a lot — and sometimes that got in the way. At one point, Adriano wanted to fire me, but his wife told him to give me a second chance because I was clever and had a winner’s attitude. It’s true: even when I lose, I make sure I learn from my mistakes so I win the next time.

Instead of firing me, Adriano changed my pay structure from a fixed salary to a performance-based one to motivate me, and in a single month, my salary went from 240,000 lira ($137) to 2.4 million lira ($1,375). After that, I worked like crazy. But it didn’t last long: a few months later I quit, because I wanted to start my own brand. Adriano didn’t want to let me go, so he proposed we start Diesel together. We did, in 1978.

Rosso with Adriano Goldschmied in Breganze.

Adriano was very well known in the Italian fashion industry back then, and thanks to him, doors opened for me. I started traveling to trade shows and meeting customers from all over the world — Los Angeles, Helsinki, Stockholm, Berlin, New York, Tokyo. We also bought and launched many other brands, like Replay, King Jeans, Viavai, Hot Product and Martin Guy, and that’s how the Genius Group was born. It was a real education.

I worked day and night on eight different lines, eight different collections. I took care of the product side and made sure everything got delivered, while my partner was in charge of design. Eventually I got tired of working on all those brands, so I sold my stakes in the Genius Group back to Adriano and, in 1985, bought 100% of Diesel.

That’s when I really started doing things my way. It wasn’t easy, but I was so convinced of what Diesel could become that I never gave up. I drove all over Europe with nothing but samples in my bag. Around that time, I also started making jeans from denim scraps. Some stores sent them back, convinced we had made a mistake and shipped them old trousers.

A truck Rosso drove in the early years of Diesel to deliver samples and collections all over Europe.

It took Italy a while to understand Diesel. The 1980s were the Paninari years, and they all wore the same uniform: puffer jackets and Levi’s. My Italian agents begged me to make the collections more commercial. I refused. That’s why Diesel was always more successful abroad than at home. My first wholesale customers were Fred Segal in Los Angeles, Henry Lehr in New York, Mario’s in Seattle, and Riccardi in Boston.

Diesel was one of the first companies with a truly global mindset. The French thought we were French, the Americans thought we were American, the Germans thought we were German. And so on.

I couldn’t find Italians who understood my way of thinking, so I started hiring people I met on the street, in bars, at Studio 54. Wherever I traveled, if I met someone who matched my philosophy, I brought them to Italy to work with me. People with different backgrounds, different education, different religions — and we all spoke English. That’s why the product was global from day one.

Opening of a Diesel store in Milan in the late ’90s.

The first Diesel store opened in 1996 in Lexington, New York.

I could go on for hours. I could talk about the crazy graphic designer I met in London who ended up creating the Diesel “Only the Brave” logo with the metropolitan punk, or the countless campaigns we dreamt up. There’s just so much to cover.

A documentary on the story of my life called Be Brave, directed by Francesco Carrozzini, was recently presented at the Venice International Film Festival, and I have just finished working on my biography written by Simone Marchetti of Vanity Fair Italy. Reading it back reminded me how much I’ve done in my life. I’m proud of it, of course. But what surprises me most is how many people I’ve met along the way. The people are the best part.

#6678. Apple Juice Bread

A simple swap from water to apple juice transforms this basic bread recipe into a subtly sweet loaf that is perfect to tear into at breakfast time with a smear of good butter on top, but it also takes a PB&J to the next level. The subtle, but unmistakable, undercurrent of apple sweetness struck me as a bit of a magic trick in a bread that, otherwise, to the eye and hand was just a soft white loaf.

I first encountered the idea at the small four-seat teppanyaki restaurant in the back of the Suiran Hotel in Kyoto, Japan, where chef Tsubasa Yamaguchi served it before my first course; it was a perfect way to start the meal. When I asked him what he did differently to prepare it, he said he just took the same rustic bread recipe he baked elsewhere and used apple juice in place of water. I was incredulous. That was it? The same amount? The same technique? Yes and yes, he said. I was hooked. It turns out the water-to-juice switcheroo gives an added taste of fall without taking anything away from the shape and texture. It’s become an instant favorite at my house both breakfast and lunch, and I expect it will be at yours.

Take care when you’re lowering the bread into the Dutch oven; it is a slightly nerve-wracking moment but a little attention is all that’s needed. You can do it!

More apple recipes here: 37 Apple Desserts That Make Us Want to Pick the Whole Orchard

Mix 4 cups (500 g) all-purpose flour, 1¾ cups apple juice, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. sugar, and one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.) in a large bowl just until flour is hydrated and a very shaggy dough forms, about 1 minute. Cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit at room temperature 15 minutes.

Set a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough, dip your hand in water and stretch one side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat 3 more times, turning bowl 90° after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Wet your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat folding process to make 1 full fold. Re-cover and let dough sit another 30 minutes. Repeat folding process and resting one more time. By the last fold, dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Transfer dough to a generously floured surface, dust with flour, and shape into a tight ball. Dust dough with more flour. Dust a kitchen towel with flour and place inside a high-sided bowl to line. Arrange dough, seam side up, in bowl on top of towel. Tightly cover bowl with plastic wrap and let dough sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven, then set a large ovenproof Dutch oven with a lid on it; preheat oven to 400°. Place a 12" square of parchment paper on a flat surface. Cut a 2"-long slit in each corner toward the center. Very carefully, tip dough out onto center of parchment, trying your best not to deflate it or ruin its shape. (It’s easiest to place parchment on a flat plate so you can easily turn dough out of bowl.) Working very quickly and using a pair of kitchen shears lightly coated in vegetable oil, cut an X in center of bread. Remove pot from oven and very carefully lower dough into pot. Cover pot and return to oven.

Bake bread 35 minutes. Uncover pot, reduce oven temperature to 375°, and continue to bake bread until crust is deeply browned, 35–40 minutes more. Carefully tip loaf out onto a wire rack and let cool at least 1 hour before slicing.

Do Ahead: Bread can be baked 3 days ahead. Let cool completely; store airtight at room temperature.

#6677. Richemont’s Jewelry Sales Rise 14%

Jewelry sales at Cartier’s parent company decelerated in fiscal Q2, after surging 24% in Q1. Jewelry maisons’ sales were up 14% to €4.4 billion in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, below consensus expectations of 16% growth, while Richemont posted group sales up 13% at constant exchange rates to €6 billion, above consensus expectations of 12%. The Richemont share price was down 6% in morning trading.

Sales at the specialty watchmakers division, including Piaget, IWC Schaffhausen and Jaeger-LeCoultre, rose 12%, smashing consensus expectations of 4% — a “major positive surprise”, as Bernstein analyst Luca Solca put it. Second-quarter sales in the conglomerate’s “other houses” division, which includes Chloé and Alaïa, were up 9%.

By geography, Richemont sales in the Americas were up 19% in Q2, Europe was up 15%, Asia-Pacific increased by 10%, and Japan rose by 23%. The Middle East and Africa were down 7%, significantly missing expectations of 4% growth.

China’s macro environment has been a major drag on luxury’s third-quarter earnings. Richemont was not immune to the challenges in the Mainland China market but is seeing growth in Greater China overall. “The confidence factor in mainland China is still not at its all-time high. We still see some rather soft business, although stable,” Richemont CEO Nicolas Bos said during a media call on Friday. “What’s interesting is that the trends in Greater China, particularly in Hong Kong and Macau, are extremely positive, so the Chinese clientele as a whole is really showing positive trends.”

Richemont chairman Johann Rupert, who was on the call, also noted the group’s difficulties in China. “ If anybody thinks we're less affected by [market conditions in] China, on the contrary. I’ll give you, for instance, Jaeger-LeCoultre is down 46% in China, yet 17% up for the year. So the rest of the world did so well that they could absorb China. Very good management and excellent products.”

Meanwhile, Alaïa has yet to appoint a new creative director following the departure of Pieter Mulier in March. Asked to comment on the timing for a successor appointment, Bos said: “The maison is doing very well. We have very good momentum and dynamics, and we had a beautiful presentation this September that was completely driven by the team in the studio, which was highly appreciated and successful. So we take our time. Alaïa is very much a maison that’s built on the long-term, and we believe there is a timeless style.” The executive declined to comment on speculation surrounding possible creative changes at Chloé.

Alexa Chung photographed for Chloé’s Resort 2027 campaign.

He also declined to comment on “any rumors that have to do with other companies” when asked to confirm Richemont’s involvement in discussions to join a consortium bidding for De Beers.

As British mining group Anglo American seeks to sell its 85% stake in De Beers, Bloomberg reported on October 15 that Richemont participated in talks.

Johann Rupert’s son,  Anton Rupert, participated in the earnings call for the first time since being appointed Richemont co-deputy chairman in September.  When asked during the media call when he will hand over his post to his son, Johann Rupert replied with a laugh: “Whenever I want to. Do you think I should?” He continued: “ I’m definitely not wedded to this. We’re having fun. I’m leaving a lot of decisions.”

Despite the slowdown, Richemont remains the best-in-class in this season’s earnings calendar. On why Richemont is doing so well, Johann Rupert said: “ That’s really due to already having handed over a lot to Nicolas [Bos], Louis Ferla at Cartier, and Anton [...]. The transitions have already taken place. Cartier, Van Cleef, and Jaeger-LeCoultre are run by different people. And maybe we’re doing better because we have a better system and a culture of collegiality[...].  And we have a pretty good idea where we’re going to be in three years’ time. That gives all of our colleagues a sense of purpose.”

Analysts had anticipated a decline in third-quarter growth, but the reality turned out worse than expected. LVMH reported a sales increase of 1% in Q3; Kering sales were down 1%. Meanwhile, Hermès sales were up 4.3%, the Prada brand reported sales up 1% and Miu Miu down 3%; the Moncler brand was down 1%; Burberry reported a 4% rise in second-quarter comparable store sales and the Zegna brand was up 8.2%.

“Richemont continues to be head and shoulders above the rest of the major luxury peers,” Bernstein’s Solca wrote in a note. “The recovery in profit margins on the back of lower gold prices and abating currency headwinds is particularly reassuring.”

#6676. 31 Thanksgiving Pies Worth a Second Slice at Breakfast

Some people will happily eat a slice of cheesecake after Thanksgiving dinner. We respect that. But this list of Thanksgiving pie recipes is for those of us who already have our forks poised over the pie table, whipped cream at the ready.

You’ll find the classics: silky pumpkin pie, gooey pecan pie, and apple pie with a double crust and another with cinnamon crumble. Then things get interesting: cranberry meringue with lime-sharpened curd, butterscotch custard with a blanket of toasted marshmallow, a pecan cream pie that doesn’t know when to stop layering. We’ve also got chilled chocolate pies, citrusy custards, and more than a few excellent candidates for breakfast the next morning.

Need more inspiration? Browse our favorite pie recipes or the rest of our Thanksgiving desserts. For help with the pastry, check out our guide to making better pie or the best store-bought pie crusts.

Silky pumpkin custard, a buttery, flaky crust, and just the right amount of warming spice. Maple syrup and vanilla bring extra depth to this Thanksgiving classic, which has converted more than a few pumpkin pie skeptics.

A beautiful lattice crust is just the introduction. Beneath it, Honeycrisp apples meet smoky burnt-sugar caramel and a generous pour of bourbon. Give this pie plenty of time to cool before slicing.

“This old Gramma has been baking pies for MANY years and this is by far the best pecan pie recipe I have ever used,” wrote one of our readers. Gramma from Chattanooga, Tennessee, we salute you.

That crimson cranberry-lime curd is as tart and punchy as it looks; a billowing meringue cap supplies the sweetness. Start the day before serving so the filling has ample time to set.

Claire Saffitz’s deep-dish apple pie builds flavor with reduced cider, vanilla, and cardamom. Sweet-tart Pink Ladies are our first choice for the filling, but plenty of other excellent baking apples work.

If pecan pie and cream pie had a very ambitious child, this would be it. A nut-packed base, brown sugar custard, tangy whipped cream, and candied pecans make each slice a four-layer event.

Detroit’s Sister Pie brings the drama with a flaky crust, dark chocolate ganache, salty-sweet butterscotch custard, and a homemade marshmallow topping toasted to golden peaks. It’s a project, but what a payoff.

This classic Gourmet dessert makes a compelling case for ousting apples at Thanksgiving (jk, obviously you have to make both). Firm-ripe Anjou or Bartlett pears, a little nutmeg, and a flaky lattice crust are all it takes.

Fresh ginger and a trio of warming spices bring depth to the sweet potato custard. The coup de grâce: a cloud of marshmallow-spiked whipped cream that gives sweet potato casserole some dessert-table competition.

The lemon filling means business—it gets the zest of four whole lemons. A towering crown of toasted meringue brings the drama, but you can break up the work over a few days.

For anyone who prefers streusel to a pastry lattice, this is your pie. A thick layer of cinnamon-spiced apples settles beneath a buttery crumb topping. A scoop of vanilla ice cream is highly encouraged.

Alison Roman’s Southern-style custard pie brings lemon zest, tangy buttermilk, and optional saffron to a tender, flaky crust. The saffron adds a delicate floral note and gives the filling its golden glow.

Inspired by the author’s Filipino family holiday traditions, this striking purple pie uses jarred ube halaya and coconut milk for a silky filling. A pearly marshmallow whip makes it look positively regal.

Think giant peanut butter cup + graham cracker crust. A fudgy chocolate layer sits beneath airy peanut butter mousse. This isn’t the time for drippy natural peanut butter; the conventional creamy stuff gives the filling its velvety texture.

Coffee ice cream, bourbon fudge, toasted pecans, and an Oreo crust make a gloriously rich frozen pie. Assemble it up to four days ahead and save that precious oven space for Thanksgiving dinner.

Maple syrup sweetens the warmly spiced pumpkin custard, while a toasty oat-flour crust makes this Gourmet adaptation a welcome gluten-free alternative. Use certified gluten-free oat flour and a labeled gluten-free flour blend.

This pecan pie’s dating app profile would read: “Gooey brown sugar filling, bittersweet chocolate throughout, cocoa crust, fluffy chocolate cream on top.” Are we swiping right? Obviously.

A tart, silky filling and billows of whipped cream make this pie a welcome break from all the brown sugar and spice. An egg yolk in the graham cracker crust helps it hold together for clean slices.

This Pennsylvania Dutch specialty is all about molasses: dark, sticky, and delicious beneath a crumbly topping that bakes into a striking marbled surface. A spoonful of whipped cream makes a fine companion.

What makes this British classic so brilliant? Instead of canned dulce de leche, we make a deep, chewy caramel sauce and add a layer of salted nuts. Bananas and whipped cream take it home.

Inspired by Greek bougatsa, this skillet-baked pie uses rumpled sheets of phyllo instead of traditional pastry. Don’t sweat the tears and folds; they’re what give the cinnamon-scented custard pie its dramatic, shatteringly crisp top.

A salty-sweet peanut-and-graham-cracker crust, banana-packed custard, and a mountain of whipped cream. The peanut topping makes this especially good for anyone who believes banana pudding could use a little crunch.

Imagine pumpkin pie with pecan pie’s best feature: that crunchy, candied nut topping. Now spike the custard with rye whiskey and deepen the crust’s flavor with rye flour. The best of both worlds, indeed.

This Southern specialty folds chocolate chips, bourbon, and your choice of pecans or walnuts into a gooey brown sugar filling. A generous pinch of salt keeps all that sweetness in check.

Before you ask: Yes, it’s dessert. No, there’s no chopped meat in this version. Instead, you get a glorious jumble of dried fruits, apples, warm spices, and rum tucked beneath a golden lattice crust. Prepare the filling at least 24 hours before assembly, or freeze it up to three months ahead.

Cherries at Thanksgiving? Absolutely, when you’re using frozen fruit. Almond flour makes the pastry especially tender, while lime zest brightens the tart cherry filling. A classic double-crust pie worth saving a slice of for breakfast.

#6675. Baked Feta Bites

Baked feta pasta took the world by storm, and once we tried it, we knew we couldn’t stop at just the classic viral recipe. We created these baked feta bites to be the perfect no-fuss holiday appetizer, capturing all of the same flavors as the OG. Thanks to easy, store-bought ingredients, these flaky, flavor-packed bites are perfect for any last-minute party planning.

The puff pastry:Puff pastry can be a game-changer in appetizer recipes, and selecting the right one is essential. Because your choice of puff pastry determines the overall texture, we recommend opting for as high a quality as you can find. Brands like Taste of Inspirations, Pepperidge Farm, or Dufour offer excellent options that guarantee a delicate, flaky crust that will elevate your bites to a whole new level of perfection.

Speaking of, we understand that achieving flawlessly cut squares can be a daunting task. Here’s a quick guide to ensure your squares are uniform: On a lightly floured surface, roll out the puff pastry sheets, smoothing out any creases. Using a chef’s knife, cut your pastry in half crosswise, then each piece in half crosswise again, so you have 4 strips of pastry. Cut those in half lengthwise, then cut each piece into 3 squares, until you have 24 squares.

How to make baked feta bites:Once you’ve got your pastry squares, you can begin assembling your bites, starting with greasing a mini muffin tin with cooking spray. Gently press each square into the prepared cups, allowing the pastry to protrude slightly—this subtle bump will transform into a beautifully cupped shape during baking. Then add in your dollop of jam, shallots, a piece of roasted red pepper, a cube of feta (crumbled feta is perfectly fine too!), and a touch of thyme. We love these as is, but feel free to switch things up if you like—who knows, you might just discover a new flavor combo you’ll make again and again.

Storage & make ahead:Wondering about leftovers? Worry not. These baked feta bites are just as delightful the next day. Store them in an airtight container in the refrigerator, and when you’re ready for another flavor-packed moment, simply reheat them in the oven to restore their crispiness. Want to make these way ahead of time? Bake these, let them cool, and then place them in a freezer-safe bag before storing in the freezer for up to 3 months.

#6674. Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup

Chicken noodle soup just got way more interesting. Inspired by Egyptian bird tongue soup, this warming spice-tinged chicken broth is as comforting as it is flavorful. The real star here is the orzo. Toasted in butter until it’s deeply golden and nutty-fragrant, the pasta takes on a new personality. Unlike plain noodles, which quickly go limp in hot soup, well-toasted orzo stays al dente for longer, holding its shape and texture until you’ve doled out every bowl.

Any store-bought chicken broth, stock, or bouillon paste offers an extra boost of flavor to the base that chicken thighs and water alone can’t compete with—for an even more robust option, go for chicken bone broth.

More nourishing soup recipes this way: Curried Yellow Squash Soup; Broken Lasagna Noodle Soup With Spinach; Spicy Cod and Potato Chowder.

Season 1¼ lb. skinless, boneless chicken thighs (4–5) all over with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Heat 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large pot over medium. Add 1 tsp. crushed fennel seeds, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. ground cardamom, and ¼ tsp. ground cloves and cook, stirring, until fragrant, about 20 seconds. Add chicken, one 1" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth or chicken stock, and 3 cups water. Bring to a simmer over medium-high heat. Partially cover pot, reduce heat to medium-low, and simmer until an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part of a thigh registers at least 165°, 15–18 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board and let cool slightly. Reduce heat to low and cover pot. Using 2 forks, shred chicken.

Melt 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 cup orzo and cook, stirring often, until golden brown and fragrant, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. finely grated lemon zest, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper.

Scrape orzo mixture into pot with broth. Increase heat to medium and simmer broth, uncovered, until orzo is just al dente, 8–10 minutes. Remove soup from heat and add shredded chicken, 5 oz. baby kale or spinach, and 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice. Stir until greens are just wilted. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

#6671. Homemade Cranberry Sauce

I don’t care if you love it or hate it—cranberry sauce is a Thanksgiving STAPLE. Personally, I love it. Every year, you can find me spooning multiple helpings of the sweet-tart sauce onto my plate to balance out all of the rich savory dishes. While I understand the nostalgic appeal of the canned stuff, homemade cranberry sauce is 1,000x better. It's fresh, versatile, and so easy to make. All you need are 5 ingredients and 20 minutes to make this staple holiday side.

What People Are Saying:“This is the simplest, but tastiest cranberry sauce i’ve ever made… My family loved it so much, i’ve had to make several batches for christmas gifts, per request.” -OrangeSushi

“Made this for Thanksgiving, and everyone loved it, including the ones that don’t care for cranberry sauce!! I added some fresh mandarin oranges and cinnamon to mine. Everyone wanted leftovers to take home! We put it in our oatmeal with pecans for breakfast in the morning! I plan to make this all year round instead of just at Thanksgiving! ❤️” -RedDice

First, grab a small saucepan—but not just any saucepan! Make sure it’s either stainless steel or enameled cast-iron. Whatever you do, avoid aluminum, which will react with the copious acid in the berries, giving the sauce an unpleasant metallic taste. Add the sugar and 1 c. water and stir until the sugar is dissolved. Now add the cranberries and bring the mixture to a boil over medium-high heat.

The beauty of cranberries is that (1) they readily burst and release their juices, and (2) their juices have so much natural pectin that the berries thicken nearly to jam in mere minutes. Ten minutes of simmering, with some occasional stirring thrown in, is all the cooking required. Don’t sweat it if a small minority of the berries haven’t burst—they probably will by the time the sauce has cooled.

Stir in the orange zest and let the sauce cool; it will continue to thicken. And believe it or not, that really is all there is to it. What’s more, this is a Thanksgiving dish you can get off your plate up to 1 week in advance. Just transfer the cooled cranberry sauce to an airtight container and refrigerate until the big feast. Bonus: The flavors will continue to meld and deepen while it hangs out in the fridge.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

While this version is perfectly classic, if you want to experiment, you’ve got a few options. If your cranberry sauce isn’t complete without orange juice, you can sub freshly squeezed or bottled orange juice for some or all of the water. Alternatively, if you’re averse to oranges, feel free to skip the zest and add a pinch of ground cinnamon or a couple of cinnamon sticks instead. Craving some crunch? Throw in some chopped pecans at the end of cooking.

Check out our keto cranberry sauce if you're looking to satisfy every diet, or our cranberry relish if you want a similar side without having to turn on your stove.

If you have leftovers, store them in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 week.

#6670. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.
